CONCLUSIONS The results are conditional on the prescribed reactor-network structure, recirculation setting, and ideal-mixing assumptions. Because recirculation was not independently varied, its contribution to the predicted temperatures, species concentrations, and nitrogen-conversion pathways cannot be isolated from the present calculations. No direct comparison with a PFR-based representation was performed, and the sensitivity of the conclusions to reactor type therefore remains unquantified. The findings should be interpreted as kinetic trends within the selected network rather than as fully resolved predictions of boiler flow and combustion. (a) Holding other conditions fixed, increasing the NH3 blending ratio yields an approximately linear decrease in CO and CO2 at the reactor network outlet. Relative to pure coal firing, CO2 falls by 21% and CO by 73% at 20% NH3, and by 84% (CO2) and 98% (CO) at 80% NH3. These trends indicate source level decarbonization via reduced coal consumption under NH3-coal cofiring. (b) NH3 addition alters coal combustion. With higher NH3 fractions, the ignition

by 73% at 20% NH3, and by 84% (CO2) and 98% (CO) at 80% NH3. These trends indicate source level decarbonization via reduced coal consumption under NH3-coal cofiring. (b) NH3 addition alters coal combustion. With higher NH3 fractions, the ignition energy requirement increases and the overall temperature field declines, suppressing char consumption and shifting the NO peak, the principal NH3-conversion region, and the char-consumption region downstream. At 80% NH3, heat release occurs in the post flame rather than the flame zone, and the NO peak moves to the burnout zone. The near-zero outlet NH3 concentration predicted at the 80% blending ratio has not been experimentally validated. This result is conditional on homogeneous mixing and the high zoneaveraged temperature calculated for the postflame reactor and may underestimate practical ammonia slip because transport-related limitations are not resolved. Therefore, the 40−80% cases should be interpreted as parametric chemical-kinetic results within the CRN rather than as evidence supporting industrial operation at these cofiring ratios. This study addresses these gaps through an integrated threepillar framework applied to three draw solutions (NaCl, MgSO4, and sodium acetate) prepared at identical initial osmotic pressure. Each DS was tested against two FS (deionized water and wastewater) to isolate the flux reduction and fouling imposed by a complex feed matrix and to quantify their effects on water flux (Jw), reverse salt flux (Js), and chemical oxygen demand (COD) flux (JCOD). Uncertainty Quantification and Sensitivity Analysis The deterministic LCOW framework yields point estimates that are conditioned on the mean experimental flux values but do not account for the variability inherent in triplicate laboratory measurements. To address this limitation, a Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation procedure was implemented to translate experimental flux uncertainty directly into a probability distribution of LCOW for each draw solution configuration. At each of N = 10,000 iterations, the time-averaged water flux Jw and reverse salt flux Js were independently sampled from normal distributions defined by their experimentally measured means and standard deviations across triplicate runs. All remaining techno-economic parameters were held at their nominal values, isolating the contribution of flux measurement uncertainty to total LCOW uncertainty. The MATLAB finite-difference model, incorporating a bisection solver for water flux estimation and empirical correlations for solution properties, accurately reproduced the experimental Jw and Js profiles and the full-transmembrane concentration profiles, validating the numerical framework as a reliable predictive tool for FO system simulation under complex feed conditions. The phenomenological COD sub-model introduced in this work allowed the decoupling of organic matter dynamics into three physically distinct contributions: feed-side COD concentration enhancement, transmembrane leakage governed by PCOD, and irreversible fouling accumulation governed by Kfoul. The calibrated parameters revealed that transmembrane leakage was the dominant pathway for COD loss from the feed liquid phase under the tested conditions, accounting for 82−89% of total COD mass transferred out of the feed reservoir, while irreversible fouling deposition contributed 11−18%. It is important to note that transmembrane leakage does not represent effective treatment: COD that permeates the membrane transfers to the draw solution rather than being removed from the system. This contamination of the draw solution has two process implications. Firstly, it reduces the apparent purity of the regenerated draw solution and may impose an additional organic load on the RO regeneration unit. Secondly, true irreversible COD removal from the liquid phase is governed exclusively by the fouling deposition term, which was substantially lower than the leakage term across all draw solutions. The Monte Carlo analysis demonstrated that the economic ranking is statistically robust across the full joint uncertainty space of the experimental flux measurements. Several limitations should be acknowledged. WW characterization was limited to COD and osmotic pressure, which precludes assessment of how specific feed matrix components contribute to the observed fouling patterns. Foulant accumulation was quantified through COD mass balance alone, capturing only the organic fraction of total foulant accumulation. The 4-h experimental window characterizes the initial-tointermediate fouling regime, during which first-order fouling kinetics is a valid modeling assumption, but does not capture biofouling dynamics, cake compaction, or cleaning-cycle recovery, all of which emerge under extended continuous operation. Therefore, the comparative fouling rankings reported should be interpreted as initial-regime indicators that require validation through longer-duration, multi-cycle experiments before they can be confidently generalized to practical continuous operation. It is also acknowledged that the LCOW values reported for sodium acetate represent an upper bound under RO regeneration and should be reinterpreted if a lowercost thermal or precipitation route is available for the specific solute chemistry. Site-specific economic evaluation should therefore reassess the regeneration route for sodium acetate before applying these results to a real installation.

RSC Advances In recent years, high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA NPs), composed of ve or more principal elements in nearequiatomic ratios, have emerged as a new class of catalytic materials. Beneting from the high-entropy stabilization eﬀect, severe lattice distortion, sluggish diﬀusion, and cocktail synergistic eﬀects, HEA NPs form single-phase solid solutions with abundant multivalent metal sites and diverse local electronic environments.14 These unique features provide multiple active sites for tandem redox reactions, enabling eﬃcient adsorption and deep degradation of CWAs. Compared with traditional monometallic and multimetallic nanoparticles, HEA NPs exhibit superior catalytic activity, structural stability, and anti-poisoning ability, making them ideal candidates for advanced CWA detoxication materials. Herein, we report an ultrafast carbothermal shock (CTs) strategy to fabricate FeCoNiCrMn high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles (50–150 nm) uniformly anchored on interconnected three-dimensional (3D) carbon nanotube (CNT) lm networks within 55 ms. Compared with conventional carbon materials loaded with single-metal nanoparticles, the distinctive advantage of this composite lies in the integration of a porous CNT framework with multicomponent HEA nanoparticles. The interconnected CNT network provides abundant accessible sites and transport pathways for 2-CEES vapor adsorption, while the FeCoNiCrMn nanoparticles oﬀer chemically diverse metal active sites that facilitate the subsequent catalytic transformation of 2-CEES. The adsorption performance toward 2-CEES vapor and the catalytic degradation performance following the direct addition of liquid 2-CEES are evaluated separately, and the underlying tandem redox mechanism is investigated. Paper 2.3 Experimental methods 2-CEES possesses a functional group conguration highly similar to that of sulfur mustard; however, its inherent toxicity is markedly lower. Consequently, it is universally accepted as a standard simulant for this blistering chemical warfare agent in research and development. Therefore, 2-CEES was selected in this paper as the experimental compound for the static adsorption simulation and subsequent elimination work of sulfur mustard. For static adsorption performance testing, experiments were conducted in a constant temperature and humidity chamber. This chamber automatically regulated the temperature and relative humidity to maintain constant conditions of 25 °C and 50% relative humidity. As shown in Fig. 1(b), the experimental setup consisted of a 10 mL outer beaker and a 5 mL inner beaker, with 50 mL of liquid 2-CEES placed in the inner beaker. A 5 mg sample was positioned outside the inner beaker but within the outer beaker, and the entire system was sealed with cling lm. During this process, liquid 2-CEES served exclusively as the vapor source, and the composite lm was exposed to the generated 2-CEES vapor without direct contact with the liquid phase. Experiments reveal that the degradation of 2-CEES by FeCoNiCrMn@CNTs is achieved not only through surface catalytic reactions but also through the synergistic participation of multiple elements within the HEA.35 XPS analysis conrms the coexistence of multiple metal valence states on the catalyst surface, including Co0/Co2+/Co3+, Fe2+/Fe3+, Ni2+, Cr3+, and Mn4+. Rather than acting independently, these metal centers can provide complementary functions involving electron redistribution, substrate activation, and intermediate stabilization. During the initial reaction stage, low-valent metal species, particularly Co0, can serve as electron-donating centers to facilitate activation and cleavage of the C–Cl bond in 2-CEES, initiating reductive dechlorination.36 This process generates hydroxyethyl ethyl sulde (HEES, HO–CH2–CH2–S–CH2–CH3),37 corresponding to the newly emerged 1.57 ppm peak in the 1H NMR spectra. The main conclusions are as follows: (1) FeCoNiCrMn high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (50–150 nm) were uniformly immobilized on interconnected 3D carbon nanotube lm networks via an ultrafast carbothermal shock method, which completed synthesis within 55 ms. The composite possessed a single-phase face-centered cubic structure, near-equiatomic elemental composition, and abundant multivalent metal sites (Fe2+/Fe3+, Co2+/Co3+, Mn4+,Ni2+and Co3+). (2) Beneting from the 3D porous CNT network, the FeCoNiCrMn@CNT composite exhibited excellent physical adsorption performance, achieving an equilibrium adsorption capacity of 636 mg g−1 for 2-chloroethyl ethyl sulde (2-CEES vapor) at 25 °C and 50% relative humidity. (3) The composite realized highly eﬃcient catalytic degradation of 2-CEES with a 98.5% degradation eﬃciency within 12 h. A tandem redox pathway was veried: low-valent metal species induced reductive dechlorination to form stable hydroxyethyl ethyl sulde intermediates, and high-valent metal ions further promoted partial C–S bond cleavage, with C–S bond cleavage as the rate-limiting step. The synergistic eﬀect between the 3D CNT network and multi-principal-element HEA enabled the integration of physical adsorption and chemical detoxication, overcoming the limitations of traditional single-functional protective materials. Synthesis of GO-Gd2TiO5/g-C3N4 nanocomposite The GO–Gd2TiO5/g-C3N4 ternary nanocomposite was synthesized using a solution-assisted method. Advanced characterization of interfaces and systematic analysis of structure–property correlations will help elucidate the relationships between material composition, surface-active sites, charge transport, and their applications. Incorporating long-term catalytic recyclability studies with comprehensive electrochemical durability testing and sustainability evaluations will strengthen the evaluation framework for this ternary nanocomposite in scalable biodiesel production and diverse electrochemical applications. 7 Conclusion A ternary GO-Gd2TiO5/g-C3N4 nanocomposite was successfully developed for WCO-to-biodiesel conversion, exhibiting superior activity compared with GO, g-C3N4, and GO-Gd2TiO5. Under optimized conditions (30 mg catalyst, 12 : 1 methanol/oil, 65 °C, 210 min), a maximum biodiesel yield of 98.74% was achieved. The reaction followed apparent pseudo-rst-order kinetics, with R2 = 0.9612, substantially higher than the pseudo-second-order model (R2 = 0.5832). Thermodynamic parameters (DH° = 81.05 kJ mol−1, DS° = 261.04 J mol−1 K−1, and DG° = −7.24 kJ mol−1 at 65 °C) conrmed the endothermic and thermodynamically favorable nature of the process. GC-MS identied methyl stearate (40.59%), methyl oleate (27.81%), methyl linoleate (20.51%), and methyl palmitate (9.83%) as the major FAMEs. conrmed the endothermic and thermodynamically favorable nature of the process. GC-MS identied methyl stearate (40.59%), methyl oleate (27.81%), methyl linoleate (20.51%), and methyl palmitate (9.83%) as the major FAMEs. The electrochemical results further demonstrated good functional stability, with 97% capacitance retention aer 7000 cycles, symmetrical GCD proles, a 0–100 mM linear response, 0.064 mA mM−1 sensitivity, and 0.19 mM detection limit. Catalytically, the material retained 92.4% biodiesel yield aer ve cycles, corresponding to 93.58% activity retention. Overall, the combination of 98.74% biodiesel yield, favorable kinetics and thermodynamics, high electrochemical cycling stability, and good recyclability demonstrates the potential of GO-Gd2TiO5/g-C3N4 as a multifunctional nanocomposite. Future studies should address long-term cycling beyond ve catalytic cycles, catalyst regeneration, metal leaching, continuous-ow operation, scale-up, and techno-economic life-cycle assessment. INTRODUCTION Previous studies have explored several routes for utilizing the inorganic framework of spent FCC catalysts. Zhang et al. used spent FCC catalysts as fine aggregates in nonfired bricks and evaluated the associated environmental risks, while Al-Jabri et al. investigated their use as partial substitutes for cement or sand in mortars.3,4 In ceramic and refractory applications, Restrepo et al. demonstrated the use of La-containing spent FCC catalysts as

Owing to their aluminosilicate-rich matrix and the presence of recoverable metals, spent FCC catalysts represent both an environmental-management challenge and a potential secondary resource. Long-term stockpiling or landfilling may increase management burdens and forego opportunities to recover the aluminosilicate framework and valuable elements such as Ni, V, La, W, and Mo.1,2 Developing treatment routes that combine resource recovery with environmental-risk control is therefore important for the circular utilization of petrochemical solid wastes. © 2026 The Authors. Ramezani et al. combined spent FCC catalysts with other solid wastes to synthesize cordierite and cordierite-mullite ceramics.6 More recent studies have extended these applications to eco-porous ceramics, asphalt fillers, and synthetic zeolites.7−9 The thermo-engineering treatment method proposed by Mymrin et al.10 also underscores the practical engineering significance of coupling stabilization with the material valorization of hazardous spent petrochemical catalysts. Collectively, these studies demonstrate the valorization potential of the aluminosilicate framework, although many routes remain concentrated on construction-material applications or a single material product. Metal recovery represents a complementary pathway that targets the intrinsic value of recoverable elements in spent catalysts. Ferella et al.11 summarized roasting, leaching, separation, and purification as core operations for recovering metals from refinery spent catalysts, while Hindawi et al.12 emphasized the secondary-resource value of molybdenumbearing spent catalysts. Hydrometallurgical leaching, bioleaching, and advanced separation technologies have continued to develop; for example, Lv et al.13 reported molybdenum and aluminum recovery from spent hydrotreating catalysts, and Pathak et al.14 reviewed fungal bioleaching of refinery spent catalysts. Advanced separation technologies are also increasingly important for improving recovery efficiency and product quality.15

Advanced separation technologies are also increasingly important for improving recovery efficiency and product quality.15 These studies provide useful methodological references for metal extraction and separation. However, refinery spent catalysts differ substantially in carrier composition, metal content, and metal occurrence state; therefore, process conditions and conclusions derived from other catalyst types cannot be directly transferred to spent FCC catalysts without feedstock-specific verification. Despite this progress, current spent-FCC-catalyst valorization strategies remain insufficiently integrated. A route focused only on valuable-metal recovery may transfer part of the environmental burden to the management of leaching residues, particularly when residual metals or soluble salts are not adequately controlled.2,3 Conversely, direct use of the catalyst or its residue in low-value construction materials can reduce disposal demand but may not fully utilize the value of recoverable metals and the inorganic framework.10,11 An integrated strategy should therefore connect valuable-metal recovery, residual-risk control, and functional utilization of the leaching residue within a single process chain. study evaluates an integrated recovery and residue-valorization route for a W- and Mobearing spent FCC catalyst. Sodium−carbonate roasting is used to convert W- and Mo-bearing phases into soluble species, followed by water leaching, adsorption/desorption, and precipitation, with ammonium paratungstate (APT) as the principal tungsten product. The resulting leaching residue is subsequently subjected to hazardous-component immobilization, porous-ceramic preparation, and loading with an inorganic phase-change salt system. This downstream route is intended to convert the leaching residue from a waste stream requiring further management into a functional phase-change energy-storage material. Porous ceramic matrices are widely used as supporting frameworks for form-stable phase-change materials because of their thermal stability, pore structure, and encapsulation capacity.27,28 Three research gaps motivate the present work. First, most reported studies emphasize either valuable-metal recovery or material utilization of the catalyst framework/residue, whereas integrated evaluation of both stages remains limited. Second, environmental-risk control of leaching residues is often considered separately from upstream metal recovery, limiting assessment of whether burden shifting occurs across the full process chain. CONCLUSION This study evaluates an integrated route coupling valuablemetal recovery from W- and Mo-bearing spent FCC catalysts with downstream valorization of the leaching residue. Using EF 3.1 (adapted), an operating-level cost assessment, sensitivity analysis, and electricity-related scenario analysis, the study identifies the principal environmental burdens, potential substitution credits, and optimization priorities. The main conclusions are as follows: 1. The two process stages have different environmental hotspot structures. Under EF 3.1 (adapted), the climatechange impacts of wet recovery and leaching-residue valorization are 1,536.56 and 1,940.11 kg CO2-eq per t of spent catalyst, respectively. Electricity is important in both stages; Na2CO3 and CuSO4·5H2O are additional hotspots in wet recovery, while silicon carbide and magnesium chloride are important contributors in residue valorization. 2. Under the adopted system-expansion assumptions, all 16 main EF 3.1 impact categories exhibit net environmental benefits; the same conclusion applies to all 18 displayed results when the two freshwater-ecotoxicity subindicators are included. The integrated process achieves a net climate-change impact of −2,257.14 kg CO2-eq/t, together with net reductions of 0.817 kg Sb-eq in resource use-minerals and metals and 37,306.47 MJ in resource use-fossils. only slightly under either option. These results show that selection of a low-carbon electricity source should consider locally relevant environmental priorities rather than climate change alone. Energy-efficiency improvement and low-carbon electricity substitution are therefore complementary. The former reduces the absolute energy demand of the process, whereas the latter reduces the upstream burden per unit of electricity. Their effectiveness varies by impact category, and trade-offs-such as the increase in ionizing radiation under a higher-nuclear-power scenario-should be reported explicitly. Further improvement could combine furnace optimization and other high-temperature energy-saving measures with low-carbon electricity and targeted replacement or recycling of high-impact reagents. These results also show that electricity decarbonization alone cannot deliver comprehensive environmental optimization. Energy- and combustion-related impacts respond strongly to a cleaner electricity mix, whereas ecotoxicity and some toxicity/eutrophication indicators remain strongly influenced by chemical-production chains. Beyond vehicles, industries such as cement, steel, chemical, and fossil fuel power plants contribute significantly.3 As a result, CO2 separation technologies are expanding, with growing research on capture, storage, and reuse to mitigate global warming and energy demands.4,5 Absorption is the most extensively studied and widely applied technique for the capture of CO2. In the COSMO-RS prediction process, solute molecules are initially embedded in a virtual conductor constructed through the continuum solvation model. In this model, the solvent is treated as a continuous medium with a uniform dielectric constant rather than as discrete molecules. The virtual conductor acts as an idealized environment in which the solute is placed in a hypothetical conductive medium. The shielding charge density distribution (σ-profile) is then calculated for the solute using quantum chemical methods. The σ-profile describes how the virtual conductor screens the electric field of the solute, resulting in a specific charge distribution on the solute’s surface. Regarding the performance of MEA, the CO2 capture efficiency increased as the MEA concentration decreased, indicating that for system 2, the presence of water possessed a positive effect on CO2 capture. This phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that high MEA concentrations may increase both the density of MEA molecules and solution viscosity. Although microbubble injection can shorten the diffusion path by increasing the interfacial area, the increased viscosity at high MEA concentrations leads to a higher effective diffusion resistance.38 This finding is consistent with previous studies, which also demonstrated that higher MEA concentrations resulted in lower capture efficiencies. Yu and Chuang41 observed that solutions with lower amine concentrations exhibited superior efficiency. Specifically, a system without water achieved an efficiency of 0.20, whereas a system with the lowest amine concentration reached an efficiency of 0.54. Its extension, the COSMO for Real Solvents (COSMO-RS), enables the prediction of thermodynamic equilibria in fluid systems by integrating quantum chemical data with a statistical thermodynamics framework. In opposite to traditional group contribution methods, COSMORS offers the distinct advantage of being an a priori predictive model that does not rely on experimental input, allowing for extrapolation to novel chemical systems with qualitative accuracy. Furthermore, COSMO-RS presents the ability to discriminate among distinct isomers, improving its applicability. Conventional laboratory methods�such as single evaporation or single-layer liquid film models�fail to replicate this process. However, urea crystallization�caused by factors such as exhaust temperature, flow rate, urea dosing rate, and aftertreatment system geometry�remains a significant operational challenge that compromises system performance.5 The SCR process involves complex physical and chemical interactions. Accumulation of urea deposit layers increases exhaust backpressure, reduces engine efficiency, and, in severe cases, can completely block the exhaust pipe, leading to engine malfunction. Although various mitigation strategies have been developed, including refined atomizing nozzles,6 optimized static or swirl mixers, and real-time urea dosing control algorithms,7 crystallization persists as a critical issue. Recent studies have advanced our understanding of this phenomenon. Börnhorst8 demonstrated through multiple UWS injection experiments that existing deposits can dissolve into subsequent urea films, influencing further crystallization. Due to structural heterogeneity in diesel SCR systems, exhaust gas temperatures vary across different sections under identical operating conditions, leading to region-dependent variations in deposit composition.14 Urea deposits formed in heavy-duty diesel SCR systems during actual operation differ markedly from those generated in laboratory studies in terms of morphology, appearance, and chemical composition. In contrast, conventional laboratory research often simplifies this to idealized models, such as single-droplet evaporation or static single-layer liquid film crystallization.15−19 Although such simplifications aid in understanding fundamental mechanisms, they fail to adequately explain or replicate the tenacious, stratified deposits that accumulate in engine exhaust pipes. These deposits formed under practical operating conditions are not only denser and mechanically stronger but also chemically more complex, frequently containing substantial byproducts such as biuret and cyanuric acid.20 Consequently, they cause more severe issues�including increased exhaust backpressure, blockage of catalyst active sites, and reduced NOx conversion efficiency�compared to the porous deposits generated in laboratory simulations.21 Existing methods neglect the kinetic processes of coalescence, spreading, and secondary crystallization of subsequent droplets or liquid films on preexisting crystal layers, as well as the resulting thermal superposition effects. This simplification leads to systematic differences in the microstructure, chemical composition, and thermal stability between laboratory-grown crystals and actual stubborn deposits. Consequently, the crystallization mechanisms derived from traditional approaches cannot accurately explain the fouling patterns in practical systems, nor can they provide a reliable basis for developing deposit removal strategies. In Melaleuca quinquenervia essential oil, 1,8-cineole is the major component and is considered the primary contributor to the oil's biological activities.6,7 Currently, vacuum fractional distillation is commonly employed to isolate 1,8-cineole for commercial applications. Aer separation and purication, the heavy residue remaining at the bottom of the distillation column is oen discarded or le unutilized. However, this residue still contains several valuable compounds, most notably a-terpineol, which plays an important role in the fragrance, cosmetic, and food industries.8 In addition, a-terpineol has gained signicant interest due to its diverse biological activities, including antioxidant,9 anti-inammatory,10 anticonvulsant,11 anticancer,12 and particularly antimicrobial properties.13 Given that this residue is rich in high-boiling compounds, novel techniques are required to separate and purify these constituents as potential raw materials for the pharmaceutical and cosmetic industries, thereby enhancing the overall value of the essential oil. In recent years, molecular distillation (MD) has emerged as a specialized technique for separating heat-sensitive or highboiling-point liquid mixtures.14 The MD apparatus is designed with a very short distance—typically only a few centimeters— between the evaporator and the condenser, and it operates RSC Adv., 2026, 16, 25557–25568 | 25557

RSC Advances under high-vacuum conditions. During operation, the feed material is distributed as a thin lm over the heated evaporator surface, ensuring uniform heat transfer and eﬃcient evaporation. Owing to the low operating pressure and residence times of only a few seconds, volatile components can be separated at signicantly lower temperatures than those required in conventional distillation, thereby minimizing thermal degradation.15,16 The separation mechanism of molecular distillation is not governed solely by diﬀerences in boiling points but is also closely related to the concept of mean free path, dened as the average distance a molecule travels before a collision alters its direction or energy.17,18 Accordingly, the distance between the evaporator and the condenser is designed to be comparable to or smaller than the mean free path at the operating pressure, allowing volatile molecules to travel directly to the condensation surface with minimal intermolecular collisions, thereby enhancing separation eﬃciency.18 In this study, the niaouli oil residue (NOR) is the bottom fraction remaining aer vacuum fractional distillation of niaouli essential oil, in which higher-boiling oxygenated terpenoids are enriched. Eﬀect of operating pressure on a-terpineol content and recovery. Operating pressure is a critical factor in MD, as it governs the mean free path of vapor molecules and, consequently, the eﬃciency of mass transfer. At higher vacuum levels (i.e., lower operating pressures), the mean free path of vapor molecules increases. When the mean free path becomes comparable to or exceeds the distance between the evaporator and condenser surfaces, evaporated molecules can travel directly to the condenser surface and be eﬃciently collected in the LF.18 Therefore, the eﬀect of operating pressure in the range of 50–250 Pa on the enrichment of a-terpineol in the LF was investigated (Fig. 4), while other parameters were maintained constant, including an evaporator surface temperature of 35 °C, a feed ow rate of 1.5 mL min−1, a rotor speed of 250 rpm, and a condenser temperature of 2 °C. The NOR used as the feed initially contained 32.5% aterpineol, as determined by GC-FID analysis. Eﬀect of evaporator surface temperature on a-terpineol content and recovery. Evaporator surface temperature is a critical parameter in MD, as it directly inuences the vapor pressure of compounds and, consequently, their tendency to evaporate.20 At low temperatures, insuﬃcient evaporation can lead to incomplete separation and reduced recovery in the light fraction. Conversely, excessively high temperatures may promote the co-evaporation of heavier compounds and increase the risk of thermal degradation of heat-sensitive molecules, thereby decreasing product purity.35 In this study, the eﬀect of evaporator surface temperature on the content and recovery of a-terpineol in the light fraction was investigated over a temperature range of 30–50 °C. At evaporator surface temperatures of 30 °C and 35 °C, the LF contained relatively high amounts of a-terpineol (65.5% and 67.7%), while recovery yields remained satisfactory at 87.3% and 88.9%, respectively (Fig. 5). Conclusion This study demonstrates the potential of Melaleuca quinquenervia essential oil residue as a valuable source of aterpineol, showing that molecular distillation can eﬀectively convert an underutilized by-product into a bioactive fraction. Through the integration of response surface methodology, a systematic optimization strategy was established to maximize both a-terpineol enrichment and recovery. The results conrm the eﬀectiveness of molecular distillation not only as a separation method but also as a practical means for upgrading essential oil residues into value-added resources. Moreover, the proposed strategy provides an applicable approach for the sustainable valorization of high-boiling compounds from various essential oils. Materials The main materials used in this study included natural dye extracts: Tingi bark (Ceriops tagal), Tegeran wood (Cudrania javanensis), and Indigofera (Indigofera tinctoria). Maltodextrin (DE 8–15) was obtained from Sigma-Aldrich and used as an encapsulating agent. Maltodextrin with this DE range was selected due to its suitable properties, including moderate hygroscopicity, good solubility, and lm-forming ability, which are benecial for spray drying applications. Other chemicals included distilled water, ethanol (technical grade, 96%), and phosphate buﬀer solution (pH 6.8) to maintain pH stability throughout the process. 2.2. Solution preparation and spray drying process The feed solution was prepared by dispersing 200 g of Indigofera paste into 740 g of distilled water at room temperature. Dispersion was carried out using a mechanical stirrer at a medium speed for 15 minutes to obtain a homogeneous and agglomeration-free suspension. The Indigofera paste used was in the form of oxidized indigo, and this process aimed to obtain an even

was carried out using a mechanical stirrer at a medium speed for 15 minutes to obtain a homogeneous and agglomeration-free suspension. The Indigofera paste used was in the form of oxidized indigo, and this process aimed to obtain an even particle distribution. Next, 90 g of maltodextrin (15% w/ w) was gradually added to the suspension as a carrier, with continuous stirring until the maltodextrin was hydrated and completely dispersed. Aer all the components were homogeneously mixed, the solution volume was adjusted to reach a total mass of approximately 1000 g, and the solution was allowed to stand until the viscosity was stabilized. The indigo feed suspension was pre-ltered using a stainless steel mesh (100 mm) to remove coarse impurities and agglomerates prior to spray drying. The extraction of natural dyes from the Tingi bark and Tegeran wood was carried out by cleaning each raw material to remove dirt and then crushing it to increase the surface area in contact with the solvent. The powdering process of the dye solution was carried out using a spray dryer. The extracted dye solution was rst homogenized and then owed into the spray dryer system using a feed pump with a ow rate of 800 mL per hour. The solution was atomized through an air-pressurized nozzle (0.6 mm size) with a fogging pressure of 4 bar and a fogging air ow rate of 18 L per minute to form ne droplets. Hot air was introduced into the drying chamber at an inlet temperature of 200 °C and a ow velocity of 4 m s−1 to provide the heat energy required for the drying process. During the process, direct contact between the solution droplets and the hot air caused rapid evaporation of the solvent, resulting in the formation of dye particles in the form of a dry powder. In this study, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics were comprehensively applied to analyze the bacterial community and metabolomic characteristics of alfalfa silages that exhibited significant divergence in fermentation quality

Two explanations may account for this phenomenon. First, amino acid decarboxylation is an important acid-resistance mechanism in bacteria: decarboxylation consumes intracellular protons and thereby helps decarboxylase-positive bacteria maintain cytoplasmic pH homeostasis under acidic stress.31 The LPGood group was significantly enriched with Enterococcus, a genus well documented for tyramine production through tyrosine decarboxylase activity during fermentation.30 Therefore, the accumulation of biogenic amines in the LPGood group may reflect the active acid-stress response of acid-tolerant lactic acid-fermenting bacteria rather than extensive spoilage. CONCLUSION This study demonstrates that the fermentation quality divergence of alfalfa silage within the same batch was closely associated with the composition of the bacterial community and the reprogramming of the metabolite profile. The relative abundance of Lactiplantibacillus and its associated metabolic pathways appeared to be the key factors linked to this divergence. Lactiplantibacillus, together with the associated metabolites and pathways, may serve as potential indicators for monitoring and regulating the fermentation quality of alfalfa silage, providing a theoretical basis for improving silage quality through targeted micro-ecological modulation of the ensiling process. ■ Funding This research was supported by the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region High-level Talents Project (NDYB202434) and the First-Class Disciplines Project of Inner Mongolia (YLXKZX-NND-039). Ammonia cofiring has primarily been explored using either detailed combustion mechanisms in pulverized coal boilers or coal combustion reactions in fluidized beds. In this study, we performed experiments and detailed mechanism simulations of coal and ammonia cofiring in a bubbling fluidized bed (BFB) combustion apparatus (operating temperature: approximately 1123 K) and conducted experiments at various primary air (PA) and secondary air (SA) ratios. We constructed a 1-D simulation reactor, mimicking a fluidized bed reactor, based on an equivalent reactor network. We also used three chemical reaction models, the Okafor, Nakamura, and modified mechanisms, to simulate NH3 combustion reactions in the BFB. Under variable PA and NH3 ratios, NO emissions in both models were primarily controlled by NH2, O, and HNO radical reactions. Reaction

three chemical reaction models, the Okafor, Nakamura, and modified mechanisms, to simulate NH3 combustion reactions in the BFB. Under variable PA and NH3 ratios, NO emissions in both models were primarily controlled by NH2, O, and HNO radical reactions. Reaction pathway analysis revealed that both mechanisms exhibited similar characteristics for NO formation and reduction. These results indicate that during the initial NH3 oxidation reaction, HNO production is governed by NH2 and O radicals, as illustrated by reactions, such as NH2 + O = HNO + H and NH2 + NH2 = N2H2 + H2, which affect NO formation. Thus, the advanced model for NH2 and HNO reactions can better simulate ammonia oxidation at lower temperatures. This enhancement aids in bridging the gap between experimental results and simulations, particularly under fluidized bed conditions, providing important theoretical support for planned ammonia/coal co-firing in fluidized bed boilers. 1. Fluidized bed power plants typically operate at temperatures ranging from approximately 1123 to 1173 K, which is lower than the temperatures of pulverized coal-fired boilers.12−14 Thus, investigating the combustion reaction of ammonia under these low-temperature conditions is crucial. Moreover, given current plans to implement ammonia co-firing in fluidized bed boilers, evaluating the detailed combustion mechanism during ammonia co-firing with coal under these conditions is essential (1100 K). Fluidized bed simulations have been investigated using both 3-D simulations, such as computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and computational particle fluid dynamics (CPFD), and 1-D simulation approaches. The use of CFD and CPFD in simulations provides deeper insights into coal combustion processes,15−17 predicting velocity distributions, hydrodynamic behaviors, such as bubble size, species concentrations, and other hydrodynamic parameters within a BFB.18−20 However, the chemical kinetic mechanisms involved in CFD and CPFD simulations require significant computational resources,21 and, the flamelet model could therefore also be considered as an alternative. Regions with strong mixing are modeled as a perfectly stirred reactor (PSR), while straight flows without back-mixing are represented by plug flow reactors (PFR). In previous research on the fluidized bed gasification of solid fuels, including coal and biomass,32−37 fluidized bed reactors were simulated using hydrodynamics through PSR and PFR reactors, similar to the approach used in this study. Among the studies on detailed ammonia chemistry, the Okafor model38 accurately represents the current methane (hydrocarbon-based fuel) and ammonia co-firing characteristics, providing precise simulations that have been verified against other models and experimental data under gas-burner conditions. However, this model assumes a combustion temperature of approximately 2000 K, which differs significantly from the conditions in a fluidized bed furnace. Their detailed chemical model for ammonia, which improved the Konnov model,40 successfully simulated ammonia combustion at relatively low temperatures. Nevertheless, this temperature remains higher than the combustion temperature in the fluidized bed region, making the direct application of these models to fluidized bed ammonia combustion challenging. Thermoplastic resins undergo a reversible change from solid to liquid by heating, making them easy to reshape. Furthermore, their relatively simple chemical structure facilitates chemical recycling.5 In contrast, thermosetting resins undergo an irreversible change from liquid to solid during curing, making reshaping diﬃcult. Additionally, their complex crosslinked structure presents signicant challenges for chemical processing.6 As a result, although thermoplastics are oen recycled, eﬀective recycling methods have not been widely established for thermosetting resins, and most thermosetting resins are incinerated, landlled, or exported overseas.7 Research and development of recycling technology for thermosetting resins is being conducted. For material recycling, the conventional method used for thermoplastics, melting and reshaping through heat, is impossible because thermosetting resins are insoluble and infusible by heat. to design a gasication system for thermosetting resins, we aimed to elucidate the dissolution and gasication behavior of representative thermosetting resins, namely epoxy resin, phenolic resin, and polyurethane, in molten alkali hydroxide. The dissolution and gasication behavior of each resin was investigated in terms of residual rate, organic and inorganic carbon dissolution, gas generation, and carbon balance as a function of the NaOH : KOH mixture ratio of the molten alkali hydroxide and heating temperature. The results are as follows; (1) Polyurethane and epoxy resins decomposed almost completely at temperatures above 300 °C in all molten alkali hydroxide mixtures. From an engineering perspective, the results demonstrated that dilute Al2O3/water nanofluids can enhance shell-side thermal performance while maintaining relatively low pressure drop and pumping power penalties. From a practical design perspective, low nanoparticle concentrations may therefore represent a more feasible operating condition for shell-andtube heat exchangers than higher concentrations, which are commonly associated with an excessive viscosity increase and hydraulic resistance. The main contribution of this work lies in the combined evaluation of heat-transfer enhancement, pressure drop, and pumping power, demonstrating that lowconcentration Al2O3/water nanofluids provide a favorable balance between thermal performance and hydraulic penalties under shell-side operating conditions. This integrated thermohydraulic assessment offers a more practical basis for the design and optimization of shell-and-tube heat exchangers than heat-transfer analysis alone. Future studies should extend the present work through experimental validation, entropygeneration analysis based on the second law of thermodynamics, the evaluation of alternative heat-exchanger geometries Article and hybrid nanofluids, and the assessment of industrial operating conditions to further identify optimal thermohydraulic performance. ■

Hydrogen economy The transition toward a hydrogen economy has emerged as a key strategy for achieving global carbon neutrality and enhancing energy security by replacing fossil fuels with lowcarbon energy carriers.17–19 Hydrogen possesses a high gravimetric energy density (120 MJ kg−1), nearly three times that of gasoline, and produces only water as a by-product when utilized in fuel cells, making it an attractive clean energy vector for sectors that are diﬃcult to electrify, including steel production, chemical manufacturing, heavy transportation, shipping, and aviation.17 However, the environmental benets of hydrogen depend strongly on its production pathway.19 At present, the vast majority of global hydrogen is produced from fossil fuels through steam methane reforming and coal gasication, resulting in substantial greenhouse gas emissions. Photocatalytic water splitting Photocatalytic water splitting has emerged as one of the most promising technologies for sustainable hydrogen production because it directly converts abundant solar energy into chemical energy without emitting greenhouse gases.17,23,24 Unlike conventional hydrogen production methods that rely on fossil fuels, photocatalytic water splitting utilizes semiconductor photocatalysts to drive the decomposition of water into hydrogen (H2) and oxygen (O2) under light irradiation.9,25 Since the pioneering work of Fujishima and Honda,5 which demonstrated photoelectrochemical water splitting on TiO2 electrodes, extensive research has focused on developing eﬃcient photocatalysts capable of utilizing visible sunlight while maintaining high stability and low production costs. The principal advantage of photocatalysis is its ability to integrate solar energy harvesting and catalytic hydrogen evolution into a single-step process without requiring external electrical energy, making it particularly attractive for decentralized and oﬀ-grid hydrogen production systems. Mechanism of photocatalytic water splitting The photocatalytic water splitting process consists of several sequential physicochemical steps that occur on the semiconductor surface under light irradiation (Fig. 1). Initially, when photons with energy equal to or greater than the semiconductor band gap strike the photocatalyst, electrons in the valence band (VB) are excited to the conduction band (CB), leaving positively charged holes in the valence band: Photocatalyst + ħn / eCB− + hVB+ The photogenerated electrons and holes subsequently migrate toward the catalyst surface. Eﬃcient charge separation is essential because rapid electron–hole recombination converts absorbed solar energy into heat rather than useful chemical energy. Surface defects, cocatalysts, heterojunctions, and internal electric elds are commonly introduced to enhance charge separation and prolong carrier lifetime. At the reduction sites, conduction-band electrons reduce protons to produce molecular hydrogen according to: 2H+ + 2e− / H2 Simultaneously, valence-band holes oxidize water molecules to generate oxygen: 2H2O +

In practical systems, cocatalysts such as Pt, Rh, Ni, Co, and MoS2 are frequently deposited on semiconductor surfaces to accelerate proton reduction and suppress charge recombination. Under real operating conditions, dissolved contaminants including heavy metal ions, inorganic anions, natural organic matter, and suspended particles may adsorb on active sites, block reaction centers, modify surface electronic states, and increase charge recombination, thereby decreasing hydrogen production eﬃciency. Water consumption in diﬀerent hydrogen technologies Water is the sole reactant in photocatalytic water splitting, where solar energy is directly converted into chemical energy through semiconductor photocatalysts to produce hydrogen and oxygen.26 The overall reaction can be expressed as: 2H2O / 2H2 + O2 51854 | RSC Adv., 2026, 16, 51851–51872 Based on this reaction, the theoretical stoichiometric requirement is 9 kg (approximately 9 L) of water to produce 1 kg of hydrogen. This value represents only the water molecules consumed during the hydrogen evolution reaction and assumes complete conversion without any losses. In practice, however, the actual water demand is considerably higher because water is also required for catalyst washing, reactor cleaning, cooling, evaporation compensation, sampling, and other auxiliary operations. Although photocatalytic water splitting is still predominantly at the laboratory and pilot scales, these additional water requirements are expected to become increasingly important as the technology moves toward commercial deployment. Poisoning mechanisms Water contaminants reduce the eﬃciency of photocatalytic hydrogen production through several physicochemical mechanisms rather than through a single poisoning pathway. These mechanisms interfere with photon absorption, charge separation, surface redox reactions, cocatalyst activity, and structural stability of photocatalysts. Although diﬀerent contaminants exhibit diﬀerent chemical properties, their detrimental eﬀects generally occur through eight fundamental mechanisms: activesite blocking, competitive adsorption, charge carrier recombination, surface fouling, photocorrosion, crystal structure degradation, cocatalyst poisoning, and radical scavenging. Digital twins Digital twin technology represents one of the newest developments in intelligent process engineering. A digital twin is a virtual representation of a physical photocatalytic reactor that continuously receives real-time operational data from sensors and predicts future system behavior using physics-based and AI-driven models. For photocatalytic hydrogen production, digital twins can integrate information on water quality, catalyst condition, light intensity, hydrogen production rate, and reactor operating parameters to simulate system performance in real time. In future hydrogen production facilities, digital twins could provide continuous monitoring of catalyst poisoning, estimate remaining catalyst lifetime, and optimize pretreatment strategies according to changing water quality, thereby improving reliability and reducing operational costs. In the short term, internationally standardized protocols should be established for evaluating photocatalysts under representative water matrices containing dened concentrations of inorganic ions, heavy metals, natural organic matter, and suspended solids. Conclusion Photocatalytic water splitting represents a promising pathway for sustainable hydrogen production by directly converting solar energy into chemical fuel using water as the primary resource. Despite signicant progress in semiconductor development, cocatalyst engineering, heterojunction construction, and charge-transfer optimization, the practical implementation of photocatalytic hydrogen production remains limited by challenges associated with eﬃciency, stability, scalability, and economic feasibility. Among these challenges, the role of water quality has received considerably less attention despite its critical inuence on catalyst performance and long-term operation. This review highlights that water should not be considered merely as a reactant but as a complex chemical environment capable of controlling photocatalyst activity, durability, and overall process economics. The presence of contaminants in natural waters and wastewater, including heavy metal ions, inorganic anions, natural organic matter, suspended solids, and emerging pollutants, can signicantly inuence photocatalytic hydrogen production through multiple poisoning pathways. These include active-site blocking, competitive adsorption, charge-carrier recombination, surface fouling, photocorrosion, crystal structure degradation, cocatalyst poisoning, and radical scavenging. Such interactions can decrease hydrogen evolution rates, accelerate catalyst deactivation, and shorten operational lifetime. Therefore, catalyst evaluation based exclusively on ultrapure water conditions may overestimate practical performance and does not accurately represent real-world operating environments. Water pretreatment strategies, including ltration, adsorption, ion exchange, membrane separation, desalination, and advanced oxidation processes, can eﬀectively reduce contaminant concentrations and improve catalyst stability. The economic analysis of photocatalytic hydrogen production demonstrates that catalyst lifetime, water treatment requirements, and operational stability are critical factors determining the levelized cost of hydrogen. Reducing dependence on expensive ultrapure water and minimizing pretreatment requirements through robust catalyst design could signicantly improve the competitiveness of photocatalytic hydrogen production. Therefore, technoeconomic assessment and life-cycle analysis should be integrated into catalyst development at an early stage rather than considered only aer achieving high laboratory-scale activity. Emerging technologies, particularly articial intelligence, machine learning, and digital twin approaches, provide new opportunities to accelerate the discovery of contaminantresistant photocatalysts, predict poisoning behavior, optimize operating conditions, and enable real-time management of photocatalytic systems. Future research should combine experimental databases, computational modelling, advanced characterization, and AI-driven prediction tools to establish intelligent photocatalytic platforms capable of adapting to changing water conditions. In this study, we performed high-pressure/high-temperature (HP/HT) visualization experiments using a multistage protocol that mimics reservoir-to-UGS conversion, including primary depletion followed by six rolling cycles of gas injection−withdrawal (upper pressure fixed at 29 MPa; lower pressure stepwise decreased to 10 MPa). INTRODUCTION Underground gas storage (UGS) is a key component of modern natural gas supply systems, providing an effective means to regulate seasonal imbalances and short-term peak demand. It operates by injecting and withdrawing natural gas from subsurface geological formations, including depleted oil and gas reservoirs, salt caverns, and aquifers, in conjunction with dedicated surface and underground facilities. Owing to their favorable sealing capacity and mechanical stability, these formations allow gas to be stored safely under high pressure for extended periods. Gas is typically injected during periods of surplus supply and produced during peak consumption, thereby enhancing supply flexibility, market stability, and overall energy system resilience. With advantages such as large storage capacity, relatively low cost, high operating pressure, and long service life, UGS is widely regarded as the most practical large-scale energy storage technology available at present.1,2 © 2026 The Authors. Once the designed storage capacity and operating pressure range are achieved, the reservoir can be fully converted into an underground gas storage facility.3−6 In China, where many oilfields have entered the late stages of development, the conversion of depleted or near-depleted oil reservoirs into UGS has been identified as a practical and strategic option for enhancing national energy security and improving the natural gas storage infrastructure.7,8 Based on operational characteristics and functional objectives, the conversion process is commonly divided into three stages.2,7 During the depletion stage, oil is produced under natural reservoir energy until pressure declines to the threshold required for conversion. This is followed by the phased conversion stage, in which cyclic gas injection and coordinated oil−gas production are implemented. During this stage, a secondary gas cap develops and storage capacity increases through mechanisms such as gas displacement, gravity drainage, and vaporization of light hydrocarbons.9−11 In the final cyclic injection−production stage, the reservoir functions as a mature gas storage facility, supplying gas through repeated injection and withdrawal cycles. Although cyclic injection−withdrawal behavior has been extensively studied in gas reservoirs, condensate gas reservoirs, and gas reservoirs with oil rims, research specifically addressing the conversion of pure oil reservoirs into UGS remains relatively scarce. Early experimental investigations were mainly focused on condensate gas reservoirs and gas-cap oil reservoirs. Tang et al. performed constant volume depletion (CVD), constant composition expansion (CCE), and cyclic injection− production experiments, showing that condensation and vaporization processes coexist during cyclic operation, with intermediate components progressively enriching the oil phase until a dynamic equilibrium is established.12,13 Subsequent studies combining laboratory experiments with compositional simulation further demonstrated that evaporation and extraction dominate during the initial injection cycles, whereas dissolution and diffusion become more significant during stable cyclic operation, resulting in gradual stabilization of fluid properties.14,15 More recent work has begun to explore oil reservoir−based UGS systems. In Cycles 5−6, injection remains condensation-driven (NMRT ≈ 0.007 mL/MPa), while production approaches equilibrium, resulting in negligible net transfer. These results indicate three stages: (i) depletion dominated by vaporization extraction, (ii) early rolling cycles with alternating dominance (injection−condensation, production−extraction), and (iii) later cycles approaching balance. The effect of mass transfer patterns on recovery and storage performance is significant. In the first cycle at 20 MPa, recovery increases only by 3.68%, far lower than the 6.93% of the second cycle, because depletion and early stage injection preferentially extract light components (CO2 + C1−C6), thereby limiting additional efficiency in Cycle 1. From Cycles 2−6, the recovery increment stabilizes at ∼5% (Figure 15), but decreases progressively as heavy C7+ components accumulate and extraction weakens, with only 0.8% improvement in Cycle 6. After depletion (27.8%) and sixrolling cycles, overall recovery reaches 56.02%. Storage capacity shows a parallel evolution: depletion and the first cycle contribute 19.6% of the final capacity, driven by vaporization-induced gas cap formation, while Cycles 2−6 contribute ∼6% per cycle under condensation-dominated injection. CONCLUSION This study conducted physical simulations to explore the phase behavior and mass transfer dynamics during the conversion of oil reservoirs into gas storage. The process was divided into the depletion, early rolling construction (Cycles 1 to 4), and later rolling construction (Cycles 5 to 6) stages. Each stage displayed distinct mass transfer patterns and crude oil property changes. (1) The depletion stage was dominated by evaporation extraction, transferring lighter oil components into the gas phase. In Cycles 1 to 4, gas injection enhanced condensation and dissolution into the oil, temporarily improving crude oil properties, while subsequent production shifted the process back to evaporation extraction and heavier oil composition. During Cycles 5 to 6, the mass transfer rates between evaporation and condensation reached equilibrium, indicating the effectiveness limit of the extraction process. (2) Experimental results showed that the gas−liquid mass transfer increased oil recovery by about 5%, mainly during the early cycles. With continued cycling, the heavy component content (C7+) in crude oil increased, hindering gas-phase extraction and reducing incremental recovery. By the sixth cycle,

Figure 1 illustrates the process diagram of the integrated absorption and desorption system. The process consists of a 32-stage absorber and a 35-stage stripper column, both operating with 3-methyltridecane as the absorption solvent. 3-Methyltridecane was selected as a representative heavy, branched C14 hydrocarbon whose properties suit this separation: its very low volatility minimizes solvent carryover into the treated gas and product and allows easy regeneration by steam stripping, while its nonpolar character gives good affinity for isoprene, keeps the solubility of the permanent gases (air and CO2) low, and provides near-complete immiscibility with water for clean water−solvent separation downstream. A pressure drop of 0.5 bar is included in the absorber, which processes a large gas throughput (∼1500 kg h−1). The stripper carries a much smaller vapor (steam) flow and therefore has a comparatively negligible pressure drop, which was neglected; it was modeled at constant 1 bar. CONCLUSION A comprehensive process simulation study was conducted to assess the technique and optimize energy consumption for purifying isoprene from a dilute air stream representative of microbial fermentation off-gas. The objective was to recover high-purity liquid isoprene while minimizing energy consumption and material losses. The separation scheme employed an integrated design comprising absorption, vacuum degassing, steam stripping, and condensation, with rigorous thermodynamic modeling guiding process decisions. The proposed system achieved 95% isoprene recovery with 98% product purity. Recycle loops for solvent, water, and residual isoprene were effectively incorporated to reduce material loss. The process demonstrated strong scalability and compatibility with biobased chemical production platforms, offering a practical solution for the efficient recovery of dilute volatile hydrocarbons. Experimental methods 2.1 Sample preparation and characterization The biomass feedstock selected for this study was sawdust (SD, original), and the coal sample was lignite coal (LC, original). Both raw materials were ground and sieved to collect particles in the size range of 150–180 mm. The samples were subsequently dried in an oven at 105 °C for 12 h. The proximate and ultimate analyses of the raw samples are presented in Table 1 and were conducted in accordance with Chinese national standards GB/ T212-2008 and GB/T31391-2015. The sodium (Na) content in the raw materials was quantied using ion chromatography (IC, DIONEX AQ-1100), yielding 0.27% for SD-original and 2.75% for LC-original. To remove alkali metals, a demineralization process was applied to both the coal and biomass. A 50 g sample was mixed with 500 mL of 3 mol L−1 hydrochloric acid in a beaker. The mixture was stirred using a magnetic stirrer in a water bath at 60 °C for 24 h. The residue was then ltered via vacuum ltration and washed repeatedly with deionized water until the ltrate reached a neutral pH (∼7). Finally, the samples were dried

a magnetic stirrer in a water bath at 60 °C for 24 h. The residue was then ltered via vacuum ltration and washed repeatedly with deionized water until the ltrate reached a neutral pH (∼7). Finally, the samples were dried at 105 °C for 24 h to obtain the demineralized samples. The proximate and ultimate analysis results for these samples (SD/LC) are also shown in Table 1. Sodium-loaded biomass was prepared using a wet impregnation method. Specically, NaCl was mixed with the acidwashed biomass at a ratio of 0.02 g g−1 and dissolved in deionized water. The solution was then subjected to rotary evaporation. Upon drying, a biomass sample impregnated with 2 wt% NaCl was obtained. All samples used for pyrolysis in this study underwent acid washing. This corresponds to approximately 0.79 wt% Na, about 3 times the content originally present in the untreated sawdust and well below that of the untreated coal, so that the catalytic eﬀect is resolvable. The acid-washed sample loaded with Na was designated as SD-Na. Conclusions This study investigated the migration and transformation of fuel-N during rapid pyrolysis and co-pyrolysis of sawdust (SD) and lignite coal (LC) at 500 °C and 800 °C, using acid-washed and Na-loaded samples to clarify the regulatory role of Na. The two fuels followed distinct nitrogen evolution pathways: in SD, the labile N-A underwent thermal decomposition to release NH3, while the stable N-A converted into heterocyclic char-N via condensation; whereas in LC, the heterocyclic nitrogen required ring-opening to form HCN, so that the pyrolysis of LC favored the solid-phase transformation of N-5 into N-6 and N-Q and resulted in lower volatile-N release. CSTR LAB-SCALE PILOT PLANT The CSTR considered in this work is a lab scale Double jacketed type shown in Figure 1. The schematic diagram of the pilot plant CSTR is shown in Figure 2. The reactor vessel is borosilicate glass construction. This resists corrosion, which means that the vessel can handle all sorts of chemical reactions without breaking down over time. Another advantage is that the glass provides complete visibility of the process. This allows the operator to watch the reaction happening inside in real time. They can observe changes in color or any bubbles that may form. The progress of the reaction is visualized by these indicators. The control arrangement employs a double-jacketed reactor architecture to ensure exact temperature regulation throughout operation. While the outer jacket circulates a coolant or heattransfer fluid, such as water, oil, or another thermal medium, the inner jacket holds the reaction mixture. In both exothermic and endothermic processes, this promotes appropriate product production and preserves the intended reaction kinetics. Additionally, the outer jacket acts as an insulating barrier, increasing energy efficiency and lowering heat loss to the environment. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE SCOPE This study addressed a significant gap in the Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor (CSTR) control literature by focusing on intelligent temperature regulation in a highly nonlinear and exothermic reactor environment. Although earlier studies have independently demonstrated the effectiveness of model-based control, data-driven modeling, and reinforcement learning, their combined application to a practical lab-scale CSTR remains comparatively limited. Many existing approaches depend heavily on accurate first-principles models, simulation-only validation, or restricted operating conditions, which limits their adaptability and real-time applicability. This motivated the development of a more flexible, data-supported, and control-oriented reinforcement learning framework for CSTR temperature regulation. To bridge this gap, a progressive modeling and control strategy was adopted. First-principles modeling was initially used to describe the fundamental mass and energy balance dynamics of the reactor and to establish the thermal behavior of the process. This was followed by gray-box and nonlinear data-driven modeling approaches, culminating in a high-fidelity NARX-based model capable of predicting the reactor temperature response under different manipulated-variable conditions. The NARX model served as a practical environment

thermal behavior of the process. This was followed by gray-box and nonlinear data-driven modeling approaches, culminating in a high-fidelity NARX-based model capable of predicting the reactor temperature response under different manipulated-variable conditions. The NARX model served as a practical environment for reinforcement learning controller training, thereby reducing the direct dependence on a purely mechanistic model while retaining the nonlinear input−output behavior of the experimental CSTR system. Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), two sophisticated deep reinforcement learning algorithms, were studied for continuous manipulated-variable control. INTRODUCTION Following the successful commercial production of shale gas in North America over the first two decades of the 21st century, shale oil exploration has attracted increasing attention.1,2 Major North American shale oil plays (Eagle Ford, Avalon and Bone Spring, Bakken, Niobrara, and Monterey/Santos) are predominantly marine deposits with high spatial continuity and relatively limited heterogeneity.1,3 In contrast, China’s shale oil resources are dominantly lacustrine in origin, exemplified

Major North American shale oil plays (Eagle Ford, Avalon and Bone Spring, Bakken, Niobrara, and Monterey/Santos) are predominantly marine deposits with high spatial continuity and relatively limited heterogeneity.1,3 In contrast, China’s shale oil resources are dominantly lacustrine in origin, exemplified by the Qingshankou Formation (Songliao Basin), Kongdian and Shahejie Formations (Bohai Bay Basin), Lucaogou Formation (Junggar Basin), Yanchang Formation (Ordos Basin), and Funing Formation (Subei Basin).4−6 Intensive tectonic activities have further segmented these deposits into isolated sags. Consequently, the combination of restricted lacustrine depositional areas and structural fragmentation necessitates more meticulous reservoir evaluation prior to economic lacustrine shale oil production in China. Although shales (mudrocks) are commonly regarded as typical self-sourcing and self-storing rocks, substantial evidence indicates that the light oils were expelled out of the shale and charged into adjacent layers, while heavy oils tend to be retained in the shale matrix.29−31 Consequently, some of the shale layers may contain oils charged from neighboring layers.32 Therefore, tracing the origins of oil can help to predict and locate the geological and engineering sweet spots of interlayered siliceous bands or shales that contain light hydrocarbons, which have good porosity, permeability, and oil mobility. Extraction Efficiency and Pore Characterization In the past two decades, studies on shale gas samples were usually conducted directly on as-received samples because the fluids within the pore space are gas and water.47,48 In shale oil research, solvent extraction is required to remove residual oil and obtain reliable information on accessible pore structure.49,50 Current pore structure characterization lacks standardized protocols for solvent extraction duration, and the progression of solvent extraction-induced pore structural changes, whether gradual or abrupt, remains unresolved. To address this, this study employed complementary approaches of MIP, NP, and CV-SANS to track pore evolution across multiple sequential extraction stages. Due to the different mechanisms of these three methods, the results generated are used to interpret different aspects of pore structure (Figure 8). 49906 https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.6c04800 ACS Omega 2026, 11, 49899−49913

CONCLUSIONS This study investigated the coupled evolution of the pore structure, wettability, and oil composition during sequential solvent extraction of three representative lacustrine shale samples from the Kongdian Formation. The results show that solvent extraction can significantly modify the measured pore system by removing hydrocarbons from accessible pores, but the magnitude of this effect is strongly lithofacies-dependent. The two dolomitic shale samples showed only limited porosity increases after extraction, whereas the silty shale sample showed a much larger increase, indicating that lithofacies, pore geometry, and connectivity are important controls of extraction efficiency and measured reservoir properties. Sequential extraction results indicate that, for the studied Kongdian shale samples

Sequential extraction results indicate that, for the studied Kongdian shale samples under the tested DCM/MeOH extraction conditions, the most significant pore-structure changes occurred during the early extraction stages. A 2 day extraction may be used for rapid preliminary screening of similar samples, whereas a 7 day extraction provides a more conservative pretreatment. However, these durations should be regarded as sample-specific guidelines, rather than broadly applicable protocols. The additional oil recovered after pulverization and ASE treatment demonstrates that conventional extraction does not completely remove all retained hydrocarbons. Residual oil may remain as bound, adsorbed, heavy, or poorly accessible hydrocarbons in low-connectivity pores or on mineral and organic matter surfaces. The CVSANS results further show that water-accessible pore space increased after extraction but remained relatively low even after enhanced extraction, indicating that residual oil films, hydrophobic organic matter, or poorly connected pore domains may continue to limit water accessibility. Introduction The move toward sustainable energy around the world has increased the use of biodiesel as a renewable replacement for fossil fuels. Biodiesel is known for its lower greenhouse gas emissions and biodegradability, making it an important component in climate change mitigation strategies.1 However, biodiesel production also generates a signicant by-product: crude glycerol (CG). This material makes up about 10% of all biodiesels produced by weight, causing a surplus that lowers its market value and complicates disposal.2,3 By 2027, the global amount of CG produced is projected to reach almost 3.9 billion liters per year due to continued expansion of the biodiesel Petroleum Technology Program, Faculty of Industrial Education and Technology, Rajamangala University of Technology Srivijaya, 2/1 Rachadamnoennork Rd., Boryang, Muang, Songkhla 90000, Thailand. For example, GyC is a signicant chemical used in medicines, polymers, cosmetics, and electronics. As a biodegradable solvent, an element in organic synthesis, and part of environmentally safe materials like biodegradable plastics and coatings, the demand for GyC has increased in the global markets.4 The creation of GyC addresses the surplus of CG and also follows circular bioeconomy ideas by changing waste into useful items. Paper carbonates.10–13 Of these pathways, transesterication with dimethyl carbonate (DMC) has gained attention because of its eﬀectiveness and environmental friendliness.1,14,15 The use of DMC is preferred because of its low toxicity, ability to break down naturally, and signicant reactivity. These features make it a good substitute for normal carbonylation agents, which oen use dangerous secondary materials and lead to environmental worries.16 Through a sustainable method, the transesterication reaction between glycerol and DMC provides GyC under mild reaction conditions with minimal environmental harm. Catalysis plays a critical part in improving the transesterication process. To assist this reaction, homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts have been used. Although homogeneous catalysts, such as alkali metal hydroxides or alkoxides, oen achieve high conversion rates, it is diﬃcult to recover the catalyst, separate it from the reaction mixture and provide environmental safety. These limitations have increased interest in heterogeneous catalysts, as they can be recycled, are stable under reaction conditions, and can be separated from reaction products easily. Heterogeneous catalysts are attractive for industrial applications because they can lower operational expenses and reduce the environmental footprints.17–19 In recent years catalysts based on biochar have become a sustainable option to traditional heterogeneous catalysts. Heterogeneous catalysts are attractive for industrial applications because they can lower operational expenses and reduce the environmental footprints.17–19 In recent years catalysts based on biochar have become a sustainable option to traditional heterogeneous catalysts. Biochar is a carbon-rich substance made from biomass pyrolysis under limited oxygen. It has a notable surface area, porosity, and changeable chemical properties, which make it an excellent choice for catalytic uses. Using biochar as a catalyst aligns with green chemistry rules by using renewable feedstocks and reducing waste production. Biochar can be functionalized with alkaline or alkaline earth metals to improve its basicity and catalytic activity.20,21 Many studies have shown how biochar-based catalysts can encourage transesterication reactions for GyC synthesis. For biochar production, researchers have examined diﬀerent biomass sources, including agricultural residues (banana peels, oil palm ash), industrial waste (spent coﬀee grounds), and marine waste (mussel shells).22 These materials are plentiful and cheap, which makes them good feedstocks for biochar production. Functionalized biochar catalysts from these sources have shown good success in experiments at the laboratory level, with high conversion rates and selectivity towards GyC. Previous studies have mostly worked to improve catalyst performance at the laboratory scale without addressing practical implementation challenges such as process scalability, product purication, and economic feasibility. In contrast, this research establishes an integrated framework combining catalyst design, reaction optimization, kinetic investigation, process simulation, and techno-economic analysis (TEA) to bridge the gap between laboratory research and industrial application. Response surface methodology (RSM) coupled with central composite design (CCD) was employed not only to optimize process parameters (catalyst loading, molar ratios of reactants, reaction temperature, and reaction time) but also to quantitatively evaluate parameter interactions and process intensication eﬀects on GyC yield. In addition, kinetic modeling was performed to determine the reaction mechanism and apparent activation energy, providing mechanistic insight into the catalytic system. The long-term stability and ability to reuse the biochar catalyst was carefully tested. Functional groups in the BSB catalyst were characterized by FT-IR spectroscopy across a range of 4000–400 cm−1. 3.8 Reusability of the catalyst The BSB catalyst demonstrated a progressive loss of catalytic eﬃciency over four consecutive reaction cycles, with the obtained GyC yield declining to 72.04% by the fourth reuse (Fig. 16). This decline in activity is primarily attributed to potassium leaching, which resulted in a reduction of active basic sites. Elemental analysis revealed that the potassium content decreased by approximately 50% aer four cycles (Fig. 5e and f), directly correlating with the observed decrease in catalytic performance. Concurrently, pH measurements showed a consistent downward trend (Fig. 6), aligning with a 46% reduction in total basicity from 3.66 mmol g−1 (fresh catalyst) to 2.00 mmol g−1 aer four cycles, as determined by Hammett indicator titration. Although the reused catalyst retained moderate basic strength (7.2 # H_ # 9.8), the signicant decrease in basic site density limited the availability of active sites required for eﬃcient transesterication. These results emphasize the importance of maintaining both surface alkalinity and structural integrity for sustained catalytic performance. The FT-IR analysis further conrmed chemical changes on the fourth-cycle catalyst, consistent with its reduced activity (Fig. 3).
