Paper activity relationship was established between intrinsic mineral species and catalytic performance, conrming that naturally occurring potassium compounds act as eﬀective active sites for transesterication. Kinetic studies indicated that the reaction follows a pseudo-rst-order mechanism with an Ea of 55.70 kJ mol−1, verifying that the process operates under a chemically controlled regime rather than mass transfer limitation. Although catalyst deactivation occurred over multiple cycles due to potassium leaching, this nding provides important insight into stability challenges of mineral-rich biochar catalysts and oﬀers direction for future structural stabilization strategies. Process simulation veried the reaction could be scaled up and that it achieved a high product enrichment to near purity (99.9%) with eﬀective resource utilization. Importantly, this work integrates catalyst design, reaction optimization, kinetic validation, process simulation, and TEA within a unied framework an approach rarely reported for GyC production. The TEA revealed that production becomes more protable when scaled up. Larger production sizes shortened the PBP and increased the NPV and IRR. This study demonstrates a scalable waste-to-value catalytic platform that advances circular bioeconomy strategies, reduces reliance on chemically modied catalysts, and supports sustainable industrial glycerol upgrading. CONCLUSIONS In this study, a CGFS-AFAC-800 activated material was prepared by the NaOH alkali fusion method, and the efficient removal and mechanism of phenol wastewater were studied. The following conclusions were obtained: (1) The orthogonal test was further optimized to obtain the optimal scheme for the dosage of 10 g/L, time 60 min, temperature 40 °C, pH = 3, H2O2 dosage 5 mM, and phenol removal rate up to 99.90%. (2) The adsorption mechanism study showed that the adsorption process of phenol by CGFS-AFAC-800 conformed to the pseudo-first-order (PFO) kinetic model (R2 = 0.9937). The adsorption rate was controlled by membrane diffusion and intraparticle diffusion, and adsorption equilibrium could be reached within 60 min. The maximum saturated adsorption capacity was 13.22 mg/g. reached within 60 min. The maximum saturated adsorption capacity was 13.22 mg/g. The nonuniformity factor was n >1, and the adsorption process was efficient and feasible. INTRODUCTION Coal is an important fossil energy and chemical raw material. Hydrogen sulfide gas is a gas associated with coal, which poses a serious threat to safety production, environmental protection, and equipment corrosion during coal mining and utilization.1−3 H2S is not only highly toxic and corrosive but also one of the key precursors contributing to acid rain. Therefore, in-depth investigation into the adsorption characteristics and mechanisms of coal toward H2S holds significant theoretical and practical importance for developing efficient H2S control technologies for coal mines,

Therefore, in-depth investigation into the adsorption characteristics and mechanisms of coal toward H2S holds significant theoretical and practical importance for developing efficient H2S control technologies for coal mines, predicting the occurrence and migration of H2S in coal seam, and creating highly effective materials for hydrogen sulfide removal.4 Coal is an organic macromolecular polymer with a highly complex molecular structure and heterogeneity. Its physicochemical structure (such as surface functional groups, pore characteristics, and macromolecular configuration) significantly affects its adsorption performance towards gas molecules. Coal rank is a key determinant of fundamental coal properties, with systematic differences existing among different ranks (e.g., lignite, bituminous, anthracite) in elemental composition, molecular structural order, and pore development.5−7 © 2026 The Authors. Wang et al.16 found that H2S adsorption on coal is more stable than that of CH4 and N2, and that with increasing moisture content in coal, the adsorption capacities of all three gases decrease linearly, with H2S showing the greatest change. CONCLUSION 1 The molecular structural changes driven by coal rank evolution are the fundamental internal factors for the differences in adsorption diffusion behavior. With coal rank increases, its macromolecular structure undergoes systematic evolution: aromatic carbon content rises significantly from 55.91 to 91.75%, while aliphatic carbon content decreases sharply from 36.70 to 6.72%, and oxygen-containing functional groups decrease from 33.41 to 10.34%. This leads to a structural transformation of the coal matrix from predominantly aliphatic chains and polar functional groups in low-rank coal to highly condensed aromatic lamellae in high-rank coal. 2 The coal rank dependence of adsorption capacity is synergistically regulated by the dual mechanisms of chemical activity and pore volume to surface area ratio. The differences in pore structure and specific surface area among macromolecular models of different rank coals directly reflect the evolution of chemical structure during coalification. Lignite exhibits the largest total micropore

chemical activity and pore volume to surface area ratio. The differences in pore structure and specific surface area among macromolecular models of different rank coals directly reflect the evolution of chemical structure during coalification. Lignite exhibits the largest total micropore volume (TPV = 8226.50 Å3) and specific surface area (8821.12 Å2) due to its loose macromolecular structure, anthracite develops a well-connected micropore network (APV/TPV = 47.03%) during its highly aromatic carbonization, bituminous’s pore structure has the lowest TPV (5425.37 Å3). 3 Different coal ranks fundamentally reflect the synergistic evolution of “chemical composition-pore structureadsorption behavior”. The adsorption isotherms of H2S on macromolecular models of different rank coals conform to the Langmuir−Freundlich model. The adsorption process exhibits clear pressure-dependent stages: the rapid adsorption stage (0−100 kPa), the slow adsorption stage (100−600 kPa) and the stable adsorption stage (600−1000 kPa). The H2S adsorption capacity follows the rule: anthracite > bituminous > lignite across the entire pressure range. and the adsorption capacity variation of different rank coals for H2S molecules exhibited a U-shaped curve, indicating that temperature exerted a greater influence on the adsorption capacity change of medium-rank coal compared to highrank and low-rank coals. 4 Functional group adsorption selectivity exhibits clear chemical polarity

It is easier for gas molecules to overcome the energy barrier during diffusion. Moreover, the thermal vibration of the aliphatic side chains and functional groups in the coal macromolecular framework intensifies when the temperature rises. In response, carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) technologies have become essential components of global decarbonization strategies.5 Among available CO2capture approaches, adsorption-based separation has attracted considerable attention owing to its comparatively low energy penalty, operational simplicity, and greater exibility in regeneration relative to conventional aqueous amine scrubbing. Although amine-based technologies are commercially mature, their large-scale implementation is limited by high regeneration energy requirements, solvent degradation, equipment corrosion, and secondary environmental concerns.5 Accordingly, the development of robust solid adsorbents with high CO2 aﬃnity, rapid adsorption kinetics, structural durability, low regeneration energy, and long-term cyclic stability remains a central objective in carbon-capture research. RSC Advances Paper Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are among the most promising classes of porous solid adsorbents because of their high specic surface areas, tunable pore architectures, and chemically adjustable internal surfaces.6 Aluminum-based MOFs have received increasing attention for gas adsorption and separation owing to their relatively high thermal and hydrothermal stability, low metal toxicity, and strong metal– oxygen coordination environments.7–10 Among them, MIL100(Al) and MIL-110(Al), both constructed from aluminum nodes and trimesate-based linkers, are attractive candidates because they possess distinct pore environments and complementary structural features. MIL-100(Al) contains large mesoporous cages accessible through microporous windows, whereas MIL-110(Al) exhibits one-dimensional channel-type porosity. These structural characteristics can provide diverse adsorption domains and diﬀusion pathways for gas molecules. Nevertheless, the practical application of pristine MOFs remains constrained by several limitations, including high synthesis costs, limited mechanical robustness, crystallite agglomeration, diﬀusion resistance in bulk powder form, and challenges associated with shaping and scale-up.8,11 These limitations have motivated the development of MOF-based hybrid materials in which crystalline frameworks are integrated with low-cost, sustainable, and structurally complementary supports.12 Biochar has emerged as an attractive carbonaceous support for porous adsorbents because its pore structure and oxygencontaining surface groups can inuence adsorbate-accessible texture and local polarity. When a MOF is crystallized in the presence of biochar, the carbon surface may alter precursor distribution, nucleation environments and crystallite aggregation, and wider pores or interparticle voids may provide access pathways to narrower adsorption domains.13–17 These possibilities are general design hypotheses. Faster molecular transport, reduced diﬀusion resistance and improved operational stability in the present materials cannot be concluded without timeresolved uptake, breakthrough, cycling and humid-gas measurements. The combination of an aluminum trimesate framework with activated biochar may alter crystallite distribution, pore connectivity and the chemical heterogeneity of the accessible surface. Oxygen-containing carbon functionalities can create polar adsorption environments, while coordinatively unsaturated or polar Al-containing sites may interact with CO2. Such interactions are chemically plausible because the quadrupole of CO2 responds to local electrostatic elds; nevertheless, their occurrence in the present composites is not directly demonstrated by FTIR, equilibrium adsorption or CO2-TPD. Previous studies of MIL-100 frameworks and functionalized carbon materials show that local metal coordination, ultramicropore connement and oxygen-containing groups can inuence CO2 adsorption.18,19 When MOFs are grown in situ on a biochar matrix, the carbon scaﬀold can provide heterogeneous nucleation sites, suppress excessive crystal agglomeration, and improve the dispersion of MOF crystallites across a porous support. Studies of Cu-BTC/aminated graphite oxide composites demonstrate that combining a MOF with a chemically modied carbon component can alter CO2 adsorption performance.20 The contribution of analogous interactions in the present biochar hybrids remains to be established. Beyond improving structural stability, the interfacial chemistry between MOFs and biochar can signicantly inuence adsorption performance by regulating crystallite dispersion, pore connectivity, and the accessibility of coordinatively unsaturated metal sites. Previous studies have demonstrated the potential of MOF/ biochar composites for environmental adsorption and CO2related applications, e.g. in situ grown NH2-MIL-101/biochar and MIL-100(Fe)/biochar systems for adsorption applications, as well as CuBTC- and Mg-MOF-based biochar composites investigated for CO2 adsorption and regeneration behavior.21–25 However, these reported systems have predominantly relied on the deposition or growth of a single MOF phase on a carbonaceous support. Consequently, the role of phase coexistence in regulating the structure and adsorption-relevant surface chemistry of MOF/biochar hybrids remains insuﬃciently understood. Although MIL-100(Al) and MIL-110(Al) are both aluminum trimesate frameworks, they exhibit distinct pore architectures: MIL-100(Al) provides cage-type environments, while MIL-110(Al) oﬀers one-dimensional channel-type porosity. Their simultaneous integration within a biomassderived carbon scaﬀold is therefore attractive because it may combine complementary pore geometries with biochar-derived interfacial functionality. Nevertheless, the deliberate construction of dual-phase MIL-100(Al)/MIL-110(Al)/biochar hybrids has not been systematically investigated. More importantly, the inuence of biochar loading on the interfacial architecture, pore accessibility, heterogeneous adsorption-site distribution, and equilibrium CO2 adsorption behavior remains poorly understood. More importantly, the inuence of biochar loading on the interfacial architecture, pore accessibility, heterogeneous adsorption-site distribution, and equilibrium CO2 adsorption behavior remains poorly understood. Establishing quantitative relationships between biochar loading, framework evolution, textural properties, and CO2 adsorption performance is therefore essential for developing sustainable aluminum-based MOF composites with rationally engineered adsorption characteristics. In this study, dual-phase MIL-100(Al)/MIL-110(Al)/biochar hybrids were synthesized through the in situ solvothermal growth of aluminum trimesate frameworks on activated bamboo-derived biochar. The inuence of biochar loading on crystal structure, morphology, textural properties, thermal stability, CO2-interaction-site distribution, and equilibrium CO2 adsorption behavior was systematically investigated. Particular attention was devoted to elucidating how the activated biochar scaﬀold regulates crystallite dispersion, accessible microporosity, heterogeneous adsorption sites, and interfacial interactions governing CO2 adsorption. Materials and methods 2.1 Materials All chemicals and reagents were purchased from commercial suppliers and used without further purication unless otherwise stated. Aluminum nitrate nonahydrate (Al(NO3)3$9H2O, 98%; Merck & Co., Inc., USA) was used as the aluminum precursor, while trimethyl 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate (Me3BTC, 98%; Sigma-Aldrich, USA) was used as the ester precursor of the trimesate linker for aluminum trimesate framework formation. Deionized (DI) water and nitric acid (HNO3, 65%; RCI Labscan, Thailand) were employed as the reaction medium and acid modulator, respectively. Bambooderived biochar (98%) was obtained from Thai Carbon & Graphite Co., Ltd. Potassium hydroxide (KOH, 85%; KemAus, Australia) was used as the chemical activating agent to enhance the porosity and surface functionality of the biochar scaﬀold. 2.2 Preparation methods 2.2.1 Activation of bamboo-derived biochar. Raw bambooderived biochar was chemically activated using KOH to enhance its porous structure and surface functionality. Briey, the biochar was impregnated with KOH at a KOH : biochar mass ratio of 1 : 2. The impregnated sample was then transferred to a tubular furnace and heated to 600 °C at a ramping rate of 5 ° C min−1 under a continuous nitrogen ow of 20

KOH : biochar mass ratio of 1 : 2. The impregnated sample was then transferred to a tubular furnace and heated to 600 °C at a ramping rate of 5 ° C min−1 under a continuous nitrogen ow of 20 L h−1. The activation temperature was maintained for 2 h to promote pore development within the carbon matrix. Aer cooling to room temperature under nitrogen, the activated product was thoroughly washed with deionized water until the ltrate reached neutral pH to remove residual KOH and soluble inorganic species. The washed solid was subsequently dried at 100 °C for 24 h. The resulting activated bamboo-derived biochar was denoted as A-BC. 2.2.2 Preparation of biochar/MIL-100(Al)/MIL-110(Al) composites. The biochar/MIL-100(Al)/MIL-110(Al) composites, denoted as BC-n, where n represents the nominal biochar content, were synthesized through a solvothermal route designed to promote the in situ growth of aluminum trimesate frameworks on activated bamboo-derived biochar. PXRD features are consistent with the coexistence of phases assigned to MIL-100(Al) and MIL-110(Al), while microscopy reveals composition-dependent morphological diﬀerences. INTRODUCTION The rapid depletion of fossil fuel reserves and the increasing environmental concerns associated with greenhouse gas emissions have intensified the search for sustainable and renewable energy sources. Among the various alternatives, biodiesel has attracted considerable attention due to its biodegradability, lower toxicity, and compatibility with existing diesel engines. Biodiesel is commonly produced from nonedible vegetable oil from the fruit of Jatropha Curcas plant, animal fats, or waste cooking oils through a catalytic transesterification process, in which triglycerides react with alcohol in the presence of a catalyst to form fatty acid methyl esters (FAME) and glycerol.1,2 Because of its favorable environmental profile and renewable nature, biodiesel has been widely studied as a promising substitute for conventional petroleum-based diesel fuels. The efficiency of biodiesel production strongly depends on several physicochemical parameters such as temperature, catalyst concentration, molar ratio of alcohol to oil, reaction time, and mixing conditions.3,4 Numerous experimental studies have investigated the influence of these parameters on biodiesel yield and reaction kinetics. In practical biodiesel production processes, however, delays may arise due to several factors, including intermediate chemical transformations, catalyst activation periods, diffusion effects, and mixing limitations within the reaction medium. Such delays introduce memory effects into the system, meaning that the current production rate may depend not only on the present state variables but also on their past values. These phenomena cannot be adequately captured by classical ODE models. Delay differential equations (DDEs) provide a natural mathematical framework for representing such processes with memory. In delay models, the rate of change of a state variable depends on its value at a previous time, thereby incorporating the effects of reaction lag or intermediate biochemical processes.17 In the context of biodiesel production, a delay may arise in the formation of biodiesel from intermediate compounds such as diglycerides and monoglycerides, or in the activation dynamics of catalysts involved in the transesterification process. Ultrasound-assisted transesterification has been recognized as an effective technique for accelerating biodiesel production by improving mass transfer and reducing reaction time.18 However, the application of such techniques involves operational costs, making it desirable to determine optimal strategies that balance production efficiency and energy expenditure.19 Optimal control theory provides a systematic framework for determining such strategies by identifying control inputs that maximize desired outcomes while minimizing associated costs. The delay term captures the intrinsic lag associated with biodiesel formation during the transesterification process. DISCUSSION In this study, a delay-induced mathematical model for biodiesel production was investigated by incorporating a discrete time delay into the production mechanism of an existing kinetic model. The delay term represents the inherent reaction lag associated with intermediate biochemical processes and catalytic interactions during biodiesel synthesis. Furthermore, an optimal control strategy was introduced to regulate the ultrasoundassisted production mechanism, allowing the system to balance biodiesel yield against operational control costs. The numerical investigations reveal several important dynamical properties of the proposed delayed system. The trajectory analysis demonstrates that increasing delay values significantly influence the transient behavior of the system, producing oscillatory dynamics before eventual stabilization. Phase portrait analysis further confirms the existence of structured dynamic patterns in the delayed system, which demonstrates that delay can induce oscillatory responses in biodiesel concentration and associated state variables. To efficiently simulate the delayed nonlinear dynamics, a fixed-step RK4-based solver for delay differential equations was developed in this study. Numerical validation shows strong agreement between the proposed solver and the widely used ddeint method. The absolute error between the two approaches remains small throughout the

Numerical validation shows strong agreement between the proposed solver and the widely used ddeint method. The absolute error between the two approaches remains small throughout the simulation interval, confirming the accuracy of the proposed scheme as presented in Algorithm 1. In addition, runtime comparisons demonstrate that the proposed solver achieves comparable or improved computational efficiency, which highlights its suitability for large-scale simulations and parametric investigations. Sensitivity analysis provides further insight into the regulatory mechanisms governing the oscillatory patterns. The PRCC results indicate that certain reaction parameters exert strong positive influence on oscillation amplitude, while others contribute negatively. In particular, the reaction rate parameter ρ5 exhibits the strongest positive contribution, whereas the delay parameter τ plays a structural role by sustaining oscillatory behavior through memory effects. The Spearman sensitivity ranking confirms that a small subset of kinetic parameters dominates the dynamical behavior of the system. Furthermore, we have performed a global uncertainty analysis using violin plots, which indicates that the oscillatory regime remains stable under significant parameter variation. The developed delayed control framework provides a systematic approach for improving biodiesel synthesis efficiency and should serve as a useful as well as realistic theoretical foundation for the design of more effective and economically sustainable renewable fuel production strategies. Introduction Water contamination remains a pressing global challenge, exacerbated by rapid industrialization and intensive agricultural practices that release dyes, heavy metals, and nitroaromatic compounds into aquatic environments.1,2 Among these pollutants, nitrobenzene (NB) is of particular concern because of its widespread use as an industrial chemical intermediate in the manufacture of dyes, explosives, cosmetics, and pesticides.3 Substantial quantities of NB enter water systems annually, where its strong electron-withdrawing nitro (–NO2) group confers chemical stability and resistance to biodegradation, resulting in the persistence of NB in contaminated water.4,5 Given its persistence and toxicity, several regulatory agencies have established strict guidelines for NB concentrations in environmental matrices. Catalytic reduction of NB to aniline (AN) provides a valuable remediation pathway because AN is less toxic and more biodegradable9 and serves as an industrial precursor for antioxidants, dyes, and plastics.10–12 Although noble metal catalysts such as platinum (Pt), palladium (Pd), and ruthenium (Ru) have shown high eﬃciency for this transformation, their high cost and limited availability hinder their large-scale application.13 For example, a Pd/C catalyst can cost between $232 and $680 per gram,14 while Pt-based catalysts typically range from $129 to $298 per gram.15 These high costs make such materials economically impractical for wastewater treatment, and their scalability remains limited.16 In contrast, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), particularly zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (ZIFs), oﬀer a cost-eﬀective and scalable alternative.17 MOFs can be synthesized under mild conditions from relatively abundant precursors and are characterized by high surface areas, tunable porosity, and versatile chemistry.18 Among them, ZIF-67 can be produced at a comparatively low cost, ranging from $75 to $80 per gram, with moderate scalability.19 These economic and scalability advantages contrast sharply with RSC Adv., 2026, 16, 55829–55843 | 55829

RSC Advances those of noble metal catalysts, whose high costs and limited availability hinder large-scale application, positioning MOFs as potentially more practical and sustainable candidates for industrial-scale NB remediation. While MOFs oﬀer clear advantages, their practical application is limited by intrinsic drawbacks such as particle aggregation and rapid electron–hole recombination, which limit catalytic performance.20 To address these limitations, recent strategies have focused on integrating MOFs with high surface area supports to improve stability, dispersion, and accessibility of active sites.21 In this context, BC represents a suitable support material. It is renewable, biodegradable, and characterized by high mechanical strength, hydrophilicity, and an abundance of surface functional groups.22 These features enable strong interactions with MOFs, enhancing their dispersion and catalytic accessibility. Nevertheless, BC is an insulating material that can swell or degrade under photocatalytic conditions, and may scatter light or hinder substrate diﬀusion, which can limit overall eﬃciency. Previous studies have already demonstrated the synergistic benet of cellulose-MOF composites for adsorption and catalysis.23 To the best of our knowledge, this is the rst study to investigate the light-enhanced, NaBH4-assisted catalytic reduction of NB using a MOF-cellulose composite, addressing a clear research gap despite the recognised potential of these materials in adsorption and

In this work, we report a simple strategy for preparing ZIF-67-embedded BC lms, to enhance light-assisted catalytic performance. Incorporating ZIF-67 into the BC matrix was designed to improve structural stability and active site accessibility, while mitigating intrinsic drawbacks of pristine ZIF-67 such as rapid electron–hole recombination and particle aggregation. 291.05 mg of cobalt nitrate hexahydrate was dissolved in a mixture of 15 mL of DMF and 1 mL of acetic acid. A BC pellicle (approximately 1.5 × 1.5 cm) was immersed in the cobalt precursor solution and stirred at 350 rpm at room temperature for 5 hours to promote adsorption of cobalt ions onto the BC surface. Separately, 492.6 mg of 2-methylimidazole was dissolved in a mixture of 15 mL of DMF and 1 mL of acetic acid. The cobalt containing BC suspension and the 2-methylimidazole solution were then combined, and the resulting reaction mixture was stirred at 350 rpm at 80 °C for 24 hours under ambient air. Aer heating, the mixture was allowed to cool to room temperature and was aged at room temperature for an additional 24 hours to complete the in situ formation of ZIF-67 within the BC matrix. BC provides a suitable support for the in situ growth of ZIF-67 because of the abundance of hydroxyl groups on its surface. These functional groups can coordinate with Co2+ ions, anchoring them to cellulose brils and creating localized nucleation sites. Subsequent interactions between the anchored Co2+ ions and the 2-methylimidazolate linkers promote heterogeneous nucleation and growth

of hydroxyl groups on its surface. These functional groups can coordinate with Co2+ ions, anchoring them to cellulose brils and creating localized nucleation sites. Subsequent interactions between the anchored Co2+ ions and the 2-methylimidazolate linkers promote heterogeneous nucleation and growth of ZIF-67 directly on the BC network rather than in the bulk solution. This process favors the dispersion of ZIF-67 crystals throughout the porous BC matrix and the formation of a stable composite with accessible active sites.26 The resulting BCZIF-67 composite was carefully collected, washed several times with ethanol, and dried in an oven at 40 °C for 12 hours. Additional selective trapping and spectroscopic measurements would be required to establish the identities and roles of the reactive species. 4 Conclusion This study demonstrates the successful development of a biobased BCZIF-67 composite for the NaBH4 assisted catalytic reduction of nitrobenzene. Incorporating ZIF-67 into the BC matrix signicantly enhanced the reduction eﬃciency, achieving 100% NB reduction within 13 minutes, compared with only 40% for pristine ZIF-67 under identical conditions. This enhanced performance is associated with the hierarchical porous structure of the BC support, improved dispersion and accessibility of the ZIF-67 active sites, broader light absorption, and potentially more eﬃcient separation of photogenerated charge carriers. Kinetic analysis indicated an apparent zeroorder response, suggesting that under the conditions examined, the reaction rate may be governed by the availability and saturation of active catalytic sites, consistent with heterogeneous catalytic systems. In this work, a powdered Mytilus galloprovincialis shell substrate was used as a catalyst for the glycolysis of a de-aluminized PET ﬁlm to synthesize bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET), and favorable experimental results were obtained. Taking the BHET yield as the response value, a Box–Behnken response surface design was carried out on the basis of single-factor experiments to explore the inﬂuencing factors of the BHET yield as well as their interaction eﬀects, and a quadratic regression model was established. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) veriﬁed that the established model was highly signiﬁcant. Introduction An aluminum-coated polyester (PET) lm is a vital material widely applied in the agriculture and decoration industries. It exhibits metallic luster and integrates the advantages of plastics and metals, reecting 70–80% of the incident light and delivering outstanding light reectivity. At present, pesticides are extensively applied to control pests and diseases aﬀecting fruit trees and fruits, although pesticide application poses severe threats to human health and the environment. Fruit bagging technology has been widely adopted to mitigate these adverse impacts. In contrast, chemical recycling oﬀers exible application pathways and enables the production of high-value-added chemical products. The main chemical recycling strategies include glycolysis,1,2 hydrolysis3–5 and methanolysis.6–8 Glycolysis is regarded as the most promising recycling route,9 as it operates under relatively mild conditions by avoiding extremely high temperatures and pressures, cutting energy consumption and production costs.10 However, glycolysis proceeds at an extremely low reaction rate without catalysts.11,12 Under noncatalytic conditions, the reaction rate and eﬃciency of PET glycolysis remain far below industrial requirements. Hence, high-eﬃciency catalysts are essential to achieve the eﬀective depolymerization of PET using ethylene glycol. Bis(hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET) serves as a critical monomer intermediate with considerable economic value in the PET glycolysis recycling system. Commercial-grade virgin PET is synthesized via the polymerization of petroleum-derived terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol, which renders its production heavily reliant on fossil resources. In contrast, BHET production through ethylene-glycol-mediated depolymerization of waste PET can markedly cut petrochemical feedstock consumption and lower fossil-fuel dependence. Unlike downgraded regenerated PET products from physical recycling, puried BHET monomers can be repolymerized to yield polyester materials whose properties are comparable to those of virgin PET. This overcomes the inherent quality limitations of physical recycling and enables genuine closed-loop chemical recycling of PET. Furthermore, BHET monomers exhibit broad application prospects. Beyond direct reproduction of PET resin, they can be applied to synthesize diverse high-value-added polymers including polyurethane, unsaturated polyester and alkyd resins, which nd extensive use in packaging, textile bers, coatings and other industrial sectors. Against the global policy backdrop of advancing plastic circular-economy strategies, the PET chemical-recycling industry keeps expanding, accompanied by a growing market demand for high-purity BHET. Literature reports indicate that catalysts for PET glycolysis mainly consist of metal salts, metal oxides and ionic liquids. Early polyester degradation catalysts were metal salts, including zinc acetate, zinc chloride,14 sodium carbonate,15 sodium bicarbonate,16 and triethylamine.17 Zinc acetate was the rst metal acetate catalyst applied in this eld. Later, various metal oxides and modied metal oxides were introduced into PET depolymerization research, such as ZnO,18 g-Fe2O3,19 Fe3O4,20 mixed metal oxide spinels containing Mn, Co, Zn and other metallic elements,21 and SO42−/ZnO-TiO2 composite oxides.22 Bifunctional composite catalysts have also been developed, such as CoFe2O4@ZIF-8/ZIF-67 (ref. 23) and Mg-Al-O@Fe3O4 microspherical catalysts.24 Most high-performance metal oxide and metal salt catalysts contain transition metals, which cause environmental pollution and equipment corrosion during their use. In addition, ionic liquid catalysts developed in recent years suﬀer from complicated synthesis processes and high costs; at elevated temperatures, they decompose into nitrogen oxides and sulfur oxides, which endanger

mediated by the HH-800 catalyst is proposed in Fig. 14. First, Ca2+ active sites on the catalyst surface form coordination bonds with the carbonyl oxygen atoms of the PET macromolecules. This coordination weakens the C]O double bonds, lowers the activation energy of ester cleavage and activates the PET polymer chains. Such a coordination-activation eﬀect of metal ions on ester carbonyl groups has been documented in previous studies concerning calcium- and zinc-based solid-base catalysts for polyester glycolysis. The unoccupied outer-shell orbitals of Ca2+ accept the lone-pair electrons from carbonyl oxygen to form coordinate bonds, which induces an electron-cloud migration toward oxygen. Consequently, the electron density of the carbonyl carbon decreases, rendering the carbonyl carbon more susceptible to nucleophilic attack by ethylene glycol.15,26 Ethylene glycol molecules act as nucleophiles and attack the activated carbonyl carbon atoms, triggering transesterication Fig. 14 Paper reactions that gradually break long PET polymer chains and generate BHET monomers. In practical reaction systems, PET depolymerization cannot solely produce BHET monomers. Since transesterication proceeds stepwise, intermediate oligomers and dimers continuously react with ethylene glycol monomers. Therefore, besides the target BHET monomer, a certain amount of oligomeric byproducts is generated simultaneously. These oligomers can undergo further glycolysis to convert into

Shells account for 40–50% of the total body weight of Mytilus edulis, and substantial quantities of waste shell are produced during mariculture and processing. At present, most waste shells are subjected to low-value applications, including soil amendment and feed additives. Such routes deliver extremely low resourceutilization eﬃciency and low product added value. Meanwhile, the random disposal of waste shells may trigger coastal ecological pollution, which highlights the urgent demand for developing high-value resource-recovery technologies for shell wastes. RSC Advances The developed Mytilus galloprovincialis shell-based catalytic system exhibits a substantial advantage in resource utilization, environmental sustainability, and economic performance. Thermogravimetric results conrmed that the catalytically active inorganic components account for 51.38% of the raw Mytilus galloprovincialis shell mass. Utilizing waste Mytilus galloprovincialis shell byproducts to fabricate functional catalysts achieves the harmless disposal and high-value reutilization of low-value aquatic solid waste, providing a green alternative to conventional chemically synthesized catalysts. In addition, the glycolysis process presents nearly 100% atomic economy, enabling the selective conversion of PET into BHET, while the unreacted EG solvent can be recovered and reused, further improving the environmental friendliness of the overall process. Compared with zinc acetate and transition metal oxide catalysts, HH-800 is dominated by non-toxic CaO with only trace amounts of endogenous Zn and K elements. The spent catalyst can be recycled or directly applied as a soil amendment, imposing negligible environmental risks. Green Synthesis of MnO-Nanographene/Green Composite Nanoparticles In the green synthesis process of MnO-NG/green composite nanoparticles, hemp plant (Cannabis sativa L.) stalk parts were preferred as a bioextract source. The synthesis process includes sequential pretreatment steps and controlled reaction conditions. In the first stage, hemp stalks were dried at 80 °C for 24 h to remove moisture, then mechanically ground into fine particles, and subsequently sieved to a particle size of 300−500 μm. Innovative adsorption techniques such as magnetic induction swing adsorption (MISA) are being explored to reduce the energy penalty and improve the overall system efficiency. MISA is an emerging technique that enhances the energy efficiency of gas separation processes, particularly during the regeneration phase of the adsorption process. It is an extension of conventional temperature swing adsorption but replaces external heating with in situ thermal activation. MISA employs composite materials that integrate high-capacity adsorbents with magnetic nanoparticles, such as iron oxide. When exposed to an alternating magnetic field (AMF), the magnetic species generate heat through magnetic hyperthermia, in which magnetically responsive materials absorb electromagnetic energy and convert it to thermal energy. This localized heating enables rapid and uniform desorption of CO2 without the need for external thermal sources. Recent studies have demonstrated the high regeneration efficiency of magnetic composites under AMF, reinforcing the potential of MISA as a low-energy desorption alternative. Under a field strength of 42 mT, complete CO2 desorption was achieved within 240 s with 100% release efficiency.7 Conversely, MISA systems have reported energy consumption as low as 1.26−1.29 MJ/kg CO2, almost half of energy consumed from using conventional adsorbents such as activated carbon.7 Designing an efficient magnetic framework composite requires an in-depth understanding of the magnetic behavior of the material. Key magnetic parameters include magnetic saturation, remanence, coercivity, and the hysteresis loop, which altogether describe how a material responds to an external magnetic field. A hysteresis loop is a visualization of the parameters, in which it plots magnetization versus magnetic field strength and reveals the energy loss during magnetization cycles.8 Magnetic saturation refers to the maximum magnetization a material can achieve under an applied field. Conversely, remanence is the residual magnetization retained after the external field is removed, while coercivity is the intensity of the reverse field required to bring magnetization back to zero.9 Superparamagnetic nanoparticles, which are magnets composed of a single magnetic domain, are ideal due to their ability to rapidly align with the AMF and lose all magnetization once the field is removed. It eliminates remanence, thus generating a narrow or almost zero hysteresis, and enables fast, energy-efficient magnetic hyperthermia. Heat generation in superparamagnetic materials occurs via two mechanisms: Néel relaxation, where the magnetic moment flips direction due to thermal energy, and Brownian relaxation, involving physical rotation of the entire nanoparticles in response to the changing field.10 Both mechanisms dissipate energy as heat, generated through internal friction and viscous drag, thus triggering the desorption phase in a MISA system. In this study, the defective product rate is the probability of the fraction of final crystal products that do not satisfy the predefined quality specification. Specifically, a defective product refers to a final crystal product whose crystal purity is lower than the minimum specification purity. Because long-term plant-scale production data were not available, the defective product rate was statistically estimated from the distribution of the crystal purity residuals. Increasing the concentration of the crystallization slurry leads to an increase in viscosity, which can reduce the evaporation rate owing to excessively high viscosity or failure to maintain the minimum required fluidity for operating an industrial evaporator.50 Therefore, a possible alternative for practical industrial applications is to divide the crystallization process into multiple stages of mother liquid crystallization. For example, evaporative crystallization can be carried out until an appropriate target viscosity is reached, followed by crystalmother liquid separation. The mother liquid generated from the separation process will undergo the next stage of evaporative crystallization. By repeating these stages, the recovery yield can be increased without causing excessive viscosity problems. Another alternative is to recycle a portion of the mother liquid into the crystallization feed.51−53 This mother liquid recycling method is economical when the fixed cost of an evaporator is high. Therefore, defining this quantitative T-P window is essential for achieving high-quality GaN epitaxy. To this end, the present study aims to delineate the optimal processing regime, defined as the T-P window in which the dissolved nitrogen concentration in the Ga−Na melt is sufficient to sustain continuous single-crystal growth while remaining below the critical threshold for spontaneous polycrystalline nucleation. INTRODUCTION Germanium (Ge), a highly valuable dispersed element, plays an important role in many high-tech fields, such as infrared optics, fiber optic communication, polymer catalysts, semiconductor materials, and solar panels. Germanium (Ge), a highly valuable dispersed element, plays an important role in many high-tech fields, such as infrared optics, fiber optic communication, polymer catalysts, semiconductor materials, and solar panels. The global demand for germanium is growing at a rate of nearly 20% per year.1,2 Many countries including the U.S.A, China, European Union have included Ge in their critical mineral list in light of their role in national security or economic development.3,4 At present, more than half of germanium comes from lignite mines, especially those located in Lincang (Yunnan province), Wulantuga (Inner Mongolia) in China and Spetzugli (Primorye) in Russia. The average Ge content in these three coal-hosted Ge deposits is 850, 240, and 1025 g/t, extraordinarily higher than the world’s average Ge concentration of lignite (2 g/t).5,6 Currently, the industrial mainstream method for extracting Ge from lignite is based on the combustion−chlorination distillation (CCD) method. It involves the vaporization of Ge into coal fly ash to obtain a rude Ge concentrate with a Ge grade of 0.3−1.2% by coal © 2025 The Authors. In the current work, a novel alkali extraction−acid precipitation−chlorination distillation (AEAPCD) method was proposed for co-extraction of Ge, HAs, and FAs from Ge-rich coal. First, an alkaline solution was used to coextract Ge and HSs from lignite. Then, the separation of FAs and HAs was carried out using the acid precipitation method. The distribution of germanium between FAs and HAs was investigated. Finally, germanium was separated from FAs and HAs by using distillation. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION 2.1. Raw Materials and Chemicals. 2.1.1. Lignite Sample. Bulk coal samples of approximately 20 kg were acquired from a local coal-hosted Ge mine in Wulantuga, Inner Mongolia. The coal sample was sequentially crushed by a jaw crusher and a rod mill, followed by sieving with a square-hole screen (1 mm). After drying at room temperature, the sieved coal particles were divided and packaged with 20 g in each sealed bag. Finally, all coal samples were stored in a dry container for subsequent use. The results of ultimate analysis, proximate analysis (including moisture (M), ash (A), volatile matter (V), and fixed carbon (FC), all expressed on an airdried basis (AD)), Ge content, and HA and FA contents of the coal sample are shown in Table 1. Ultimate analysis was carried out using an EL cube CHNSO elemental analyzer (Elementar Corp., Hanau, Hessen, Germany). The determination of HA and FA contents is referred to

HA and FA contents of the coal sample are shown in Table 1. Ultimate analysis was carried out using an EL cube CHNSO elemental analyzer (Elementar Corp., Hanau, Hessen, Germany). The determination of HA and FA contents is referred to Chinese standards GB/T 34766−2017 and GB/T 34765−2017, respectively. The general steps are as follows: using a mixed alkali solution of Na4P2O7 and NaOH to extract HAs and FAs from lignite, the extraction solution was precipitated with H2SO4, filtered, and the filtrate was oxidized with K2Cr2O7 under strong acid conditions. Excess K2Cr2O7 was titrated with a standard (NH4)2Fe(SO4)2 solution, and the mass fraction of carbon in FAs (relative to the mass of the lignite sample) was calculated based on the consumption of K2Cr2O7. Then, this value was multiplied by 0.59 to obtain the FA content. After dissolution by dilute NaOH solution, the filter residue underwent the same steps as described above to obtain the HA content of lignite. The determination of the Ge content was carried out by using an inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (PerkinElmer Optima 8300). Prior to ICP-OES determination, the coal sample was subjected to ashing and digested with mixed acid (HNO3+H3PO4+HF) according to the Chinese standard (GB/T 8207−2007). 1665 https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.5c09543 ACS Omega 2026, 11, 1664−1678

CONCLUSIONS This study proposed an alkali extraction−acid precipitation− chlorination distillation method, which can comprehensively recover the high-valued organic and inorganic components of Ge-rich lignite in an environmentally friendly way. Alkaline extraction can simultaneously extract HSs and Ge in lignite. By performing extraction experiments with different operational conditions, it is found that the 0.1 M NaOH solution can extract 88.7% of HSs and 58.3% of germanium (which is closely bound to HSs). The occurrence forms of germanium in lignite are diverse. Increasing the concentration of alkaline solution can further extract other forms of germanium in lignite, which may be related to the fact that alkali can promote the depolymerization of lignin-like substances in lignite. The depolymerization products are mostly the basic structural units that make up lignin macromolecules or their derivatives,

The RDPFC process attains a MeAc conversion rate of 99.2 mol %, yielding products that align with commercial specifications, including over 99.85 wt % MeOH and more than 99.5 wt % BuAc. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION The section includes the results obtained by simulating and optimizing the proposed reactive distillation system with a prefractional column (RDPFC). The influence of design factors, such as the number of reactive stages, reflux ratio, and operating pressure, is analyzed. CONCLUSIONS This study analyzes the feasibility and benefits of a reactive distillation with a prefractionation column (RDPFC) process for valorizing the MeAc and MeOH waste from PVA synthesis. The optimized system consists of a 26-stage prefractionation column operating at 0.6 atm and a 38-stage reactive column operating at 8.0 atm, 21 of which are reactive stages where the transesterification reaction occurs. This process achieves an overall MeAc conversion of 99.2 mol %, yielding high-purity BuAc (>99.5 wt %) and methanol (>99.85 wt

a 38-stage reactive column operating at 8.0 atm, 21 of which are reactive stages where the transesterification reaction occurs. This process achieves an overall MeAc conversion of 99.2 mol %, yielding high-purity BuAc (>99.5 wt %) and methanol (>99.85 wt %) that meet commercial specifications. The primary innovation lies in overcoming multiple azeotropes in a single column. Despite having these mixtures in the same unit, the proposed reactive column is capable of splitting and reacting the mixture, obtaining commercial specifications of BuAc at the bottom and high-purity values of MeOH at the overhead. A prefractionation column is added just to reach the commercial specifications of MeOH, but the RC can separate the components by itself. A comparative analysis highlighted that the RDPFC system requires only 2.56 GJ/tBuAc, a 67% reduction in total energy consumption compared to that of the conventional reactive and extractive distillation (RED) process. Eliminating the need for an entrainer and its associated recovery unit primarily achieves this improvement. The study also emphasized the critical role of catalyst thermal stability, indicating that a catalyst capable of withstanding temperatures up to 220 °C is essential for optimal performance. The drying shrinkage behavior of concrete can be classified into three progressive stages that are primarily governed by moisture migration and microstructural evolution. The first stage, known as the plastic shrinkage, occurs within the first 2− 3 h after water is mixed with cement particles, as the hydration reaction progresses. Then, the early-age rapid shrinkage period (0−200 h in Figure 3) is characterized by the evaporation of free water from large capillary pores following demolding and initial curing. During this phase, a rapid volumetric contraction occurs due to steep surface moisture gradients, leading to high internal capillary tension. These tensions initiate the development of microcracks, particularly near the paste−aggregate interfaces where stiffness mismatches concentrate stress. The process is strongly influenced by curing temperature, relative humidity gradients, and the degree of pore connectivity, which collectively determine the rate of moisture loss and the extent of early shrinkage deformation. As the concrete transitions into the intermediate steady-decline period (i.e., 200−2000 h), the rate of shrinkage begins to diminish as the moisture gradients within the material stabilize. In this

As the concrete transitions into the intermediate steady-decline period (i.e., 200−2000 h), the rate of shrinkage begins to diminish as the moisture gradients within the material stabilize. In this stage, water molecules continue migrating from finer capillary and gel pores, accompanied by internal redistribution processes that relieve localized stress concentrations. The incorporation of fly ash plays a significant role during this phase, as the ongoing pozzolanic reaction promotes the formation of an additional C−S−H gel. This reaction refines the pore structure, reduces the average pore radius, and enhances their internal humidity buffering capacity. Consequently, the overall shrinkage rate decreases, and the internal stress field becomes more balanced, reflecting a progressive stabilization of the microstructural framework. Finally, the long-term stabilization stage (i.e., 2000−4960 h) marks the point where the moisture content of the concrete achieves equilibrium with the surrounding environment. Only the bound water within the finest gel pores continues to desorb gradually, leading to a near-constant strain response. The shrinkage curve flattens toward its asymptotic value, indicating that most of the capillary-driven moisture movement has ceased. Aggregate stiffness and curing temperature continue to exert minor influences on residual microstrains.

However, the hydrodynamic behavior of fresh seeds, characterized by high surface moisture and mucilaginous adhesion, remains poorly documented under spouted bed conditions. This study systematically investigated the drying performance of papaya seeds using a Box−Behnken experimental design. Initial trials showed that removing the sarcotesta drastically reduced the minimum spouting velocity (ums) from 1.94 to 0.98 ms−1 and the peak pressure dropped from 1200 to 490 Pa, highlighting the dominant role of surface cohesion. A 15 min flash-drying pretreatment at 4 m3 min−1 was essential to reduce surface stickiness and enable stable spouting. The experimental design evaluated air temperature (40−60 °C), processing time (20−60 min), and airflow rate (1.0−2.0 m3 min−1). Quadratic regression models for moisture content and water activity (aw) exhibited excellent fit (R2 > 0.99; Radj2 > 0.97) with no significant lack of fit (p > 0.05). Multiresponse optimization via desirability profile (≈60 °C, ≈60 min, and 1.61 m3 min−1) converged with experimental results (U = 7.2% and aw = 0.57), reaching the thermodynamic safety threshold (aw < 0.60) for microbial inhibition. Drying acts as a fundamental unit operation to extend the shelf life and ensure the physicochemical stability of biological materials.9 However, handling coarse-grained particles presents considerable hydrodynamic challenges. Because of their diameter, porosity, and specifically the presence of a highly cohesive mucilaginous layer (the sarcotesta), papaya seeds exhibit strong interparticle adhesion. This characteristic frequently places them in particle categories that do not fluidize properly in conventional systems, tending toward air channeling or the formation of unstable bubbles.10 This behavior demands the use of technologies that promote a more rigorous and uniform gas−solid contact. Unlike standard spouted beds, the equipment utilized in this study features a modified conicalcylindrical geometry with an atypically large air inlet diameter (9.47 cm). This specific design preserves the heat and mass transfer benefits of the conical section but significantly reduces the pressure drop required to achieve a stable spouting state while promoting a lower, controlled fountain height, eliminating the need for internal draft tubes or deflectors. The system is also sealed with a fine mesh screen and coupled to a cyclone to ensure the recovery of elutriated fines. biomaterials.12,14 Seed Fluid Dynamics The fluid dynamic behavior of seeds with intact sarcotesta (Figure 1, which represents the mean profile of three independent experimental runs) exhibited severe hysteresis and erratic pressure fluctuations. Instead of a sharp transition to a stable spouting regime, the bed presented an unstable intermediate pressure region without immediate stabilization. This atypical behavior is primarily attributed to the strong cohesive and adhesive forces exerted by the moisture-rich mucilage, which promotes particle agglomeration. In this case, ΔPstable fluctuated between 1120 and 1340 Pa across the experimental replicates (averaging approximately 1200 Pa) just to break the initial packing. The consistent recording of this high-pressure variation range across independent runs confirms the reproducibility of these erratic patterns for mucilage-coated seeds. Conversely, the mechanical removal of the sarcotesta drastically altered the bed’s hydrodynamics (Figure 2, which also represents the mean profile of the experimental triplicates). The system exhibited a classic spouted bed pressure drop curve, characterized by a distinct peak pressure drop followed by a sharp decline to a stable operational pressure drop (ΔPstable) that consistently remained between 470 and 520 Pa (averaging approximately 490 Pa). The RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Physical Characterization Papaya seeds (Carica papaya L.) were characterized regarding their physical properties, with n = 80 for mean diameter and sphericity and n = 5 for density, with the results described in Table 1. During this process, natural fermentation and dehydration reduce the moisture content and promote the homogenization of waste components. Anaerobic fermentation (AF) is an innovative strategy for the valorization of lignocellulosic streams into high-value compounds that relies on mixed cultures. AF can be directed towards the accumulation of carboxylic acids (i.e., citric (HCit), lactic (HLac), formic (HFor), acetic (HAc), propionic (HPro), isobutyric (isoHBut), butyric (HBut), iso-valeric (isoHVal), valeric (HVal), iso-hexanoic (isoHHex) and hexanoic acids (HHex)) by controlling operational conditions to inhibit methanogenic archaea. Because AF is conventionally carried out using anaerobic inocula sourced from anaerobic digesters, the resulting microbiome exhibits a wide range of microbial activities, oen leading to eﬄuents rich in a mixture of carboxylates.13 This can be considered a problem, as acids extraction from the cultivation broth and purication may compromise the cost-eﬃcient use of the carboxylates. Bioaugmentation strategies in AF (i.e., deliberate inoculation with a specic microorganism) oﬀer a promising approach to steer metabolic selectivity and reduce the diversity of carboxylates produced in mixed-culture fermentations. By introducing microorganisms with dened metabolic pathways, bioaugmentation can selectively enrich specic carboxylates, thereby facilitating product recovery and purication. Furthermore, these strategies have shown to stabilize microbial communities and enhance process robustness under challenging environmental conditions,14,15 providing a pathway toward viable valorization of lignocellulosic residues into platform chemicals. The present work addresses these gaps by investigating the AF of lignocellulosic prehydrolysates derived from steam-exploded MGR using nonsterile mixed cultures in continuous stirred-tank reactors (CSTRs). To facilitate the conversion of the lignocellulosic stream, an activated carbon (AC) detoxication step was optimized. The diﬀerential response of inhibitor removal to contact time reected diﬀerences in adsorption kinetics across compound classes. Expanding knowledge in this area as an alternative to pure cultures is particularly relevant because microbial diversity enhances process resilience to operational stresses, enables the degradation of the broad spectrum of organic compounds present in complex waste streams, and eliminates the need for sterile operating conditions. High selectivity in fermentation processes is typically directed toward a single target compound, such as HLac, and is most commonly achieved using pure cultures or genetically modied microorganisms. While these systems can deliver high product titers and yields, they generally require strict sterile operation, and, in the case of genetically modied organisms, compliance with regulatory frameworks, all of which increase process complexity and cost. In contrast, the mixed-culture approach applied here prioritizes operational simplicity, process robustness, and the ability to valorize complex, nonsterile waste streams. Although carbon is inherently distributed across multiple metabolic pathways in such systems, resulting in lower selectivity compared to pure cultures, bioaugmentation enabled partial metabolic steering toward a targeted product spectrum. To assess the presence of L. pentosus in the bioaugmented RSC Advances bioreactor, a GHKL domain-containing gene (named LP GHKL in Fig. 4), which is unique to this specie, was targeted using a species-specic primer pair.29 The GHKL domain-containing gene encodes a protein belonging to the GHKL ATPase superfamily (Gyrase, Hsp90, Histidine Kinase, and MutL), which is involved in fundamental prokaryotic processes such as signal transduction and DNA repair. Its use as a species-specic marker for L. pentosus is not associated with a unique metabolic function, but rather with its sequence divergence from homologous genes in closely related species. Comparative genomic analysis of 180 Lactobacillus genomes demonstrated that this gene provides suﬃcient resolution for species-level discrimination.29 This level of resolution is required because L. pentosus, L. plantarum, and L. paraplantarum share 99.7– 99.9% 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity, which prevents reliable diﬀerentiation using standard amplicon sequencing. ACS Omega http://pubs.acs.org/journal/acsodf Ilmenite has been extensively studied in the context of fluidized bed, especially in chemical looping combustion (CLC), considering its ability to transport oxygen throughout the bed and provide more uniform combustion conditions.20−26 The oxygen-carrying ability of ilmenite bed particles is associated with the migration of Fe from the core to the surface of the bed particles.27 Under oxidized conditions, Fe can exist as pseudobrookite (Fe2TiO5) or hematite (Fe2O3), whereas under reduced conditions, it can be found as ilmenite (FeTiO3) or magnetite (Fe3O4).28 However, the outward migration of Fe creates porous regions within the bed particles’ core, which eventually compromises their structural integrity and mechanical stability.27,29 The performance of ilmenite bed particles in the process is significantly influenced by the formation of the bed particle layer.20,29,30 The layer formation, which is a well-documented phenomenon in fluidized bed processes, arises from the interaction between the bed material and the ash-forming matter in the biomass fuel.31−36 There are both challenges and opportunities associated with the formation of the bed particle layer. In some instances, this layer can lead to agglomeration of the bed particles.37,38 Bed particle fragmentation and deposition of the fine fragments in the downstream facilities (e.g., cyclones and

and opportunities associated with the formation of the bed particle layer. In some instances, this layer can lead to agglomeration of the bed particles.37,38 Bed particle fragmentation and deposition of the fine fragments in the downstream facilities (e.g., cyclones and return legs) pose further problems associated with bed particle layer formation.39 However, a positive effect of the bed particle layer on tar reduction has been reported in the thermal conversion of biomass in fluidized beds.40 The formation of the bed particle layer can occur through two distin mechanisms, the “reaction mechanism” and the “deposition mechanism”, each resulting in specific bed particle layer characteristics. In the reaction mechanism, the bed particle layer forms through the direct reaction of fuel-derived Ca- and K-rich compounds with the bed material, resulting in a Casilicate-rich layer on the bed particle surface. This occurs when biomass rich in Ca and K (e.g., woody biomass) is used.31−33,41,42 In the deposition mechanism, the bed particle layer develops through the accumulation of ash-derived lowtemperature melting silicates and/or phosphates on the bed particle surface. This can occur when the biomass fuel is rich in Si, and/or P.43−45 Bed particle layer formation on ilmenite bed particles utilized in fluidized bed combustion

This can occur when the biomass fuel is rich in Si, and/or P.43−45 Bed particle layer formation on ilmenite bed particles utilized in fluidized bed combustion of various woody biomass fuels (which are characterized by high Ca and K contents) has been extensively studied and documented in the literature.20,27,29,30 In these cases, bed particle layer formation begins with Ca-rich coarse ash particles (primarily present as CaO at typical combustion temperatures)46 adhering to the bed particle surface upon impact. Consequently, Ca in its ionic form diffuses into the bed particle. The diffused Ca then reacts with the bed material to form Ca-titanate, which is referred to as the inner layer. Simultaneously, Fe from the bed material migrates toward the bed particle surface, establishing an Fe-rich outer layer, while regions depleted of Fe become porous. This outer layer is not uniformly distributed across different surface morphologies but is mainly observed on the convex areas. In conjunction with the iron migration, fuel-derived K compounds diffuse into the bed particle core, forming K-titanate, which is predominantly found in the Fe-depleted (porous) regions. two Ca-rich layers can be identified in the EDS elemental mappings: one from the Ca−Ti-rich inner layer and the other from the Ca−P−Mg-K-rich outer layer. Based on the findings of this study, the homogeneous outer layer that forms on the bed particles, covering both convex and concave areas, prevents the outward migration of Fe. As a result, only a thin, porous zone is observed in ilmenite bed particles used with CL, which forms during the initial stage of the process before the outer layer has fully developed. However, gaseous K can still penetrate into the bed particle core through the cracks which are mainly connected to the concaves on the bed particle surface. In contrast, when woody biomass is used, Fe can migrate to the surface through concave areas where the outer layer is absent, allowing the development of porous regions to persist throughout the process. Consequently, under identical conditions, it is expected that ilmenite bed particles used in fluidized bed combustion of woody biomass will exhibit a significantly higher volume fraction of porous areas compared to those used with CL. In a previous study on ilmenite bed particles using a tubular furnace with synthetic ash, it was shown that in the presence of KH2PO4, a dense KPO3 layer forms on the surface of bed particles. This layer impedes oxygen transport, thereby reducing ilmenite’s reactivity and its overall effectiveness as an oxygen carrier in CLC.49 Similarly, the oxygen-carrying capacity of ilmenite bed particles is theoretically expected to be compromised when CL is used, due to the limited transport of Fe to the bed particle surface.20 However, a detailed study of the oxygen-carrying capacity of ilmenite bed particles in fluidized bed combustion of CL, in future research, would provide experimental evidence to validate this expectation. 4. the findings, the following conclusions can be drawn: • In the initial stage of the process, the bed particle layer formation is governed by the reaction of the bed material with fine fuel-derived Ca-rich particles formed via attrition. The inner layer is developed at this stage and is mainly composed of Ca and Ti. • After a few hours of operation, the outer layer develops through the direct adhesion of partially molten individual fuel-derived bed ash particles containing Ca, P, Mg, and K, which subsequently controls the ongoing formation of the bed particle layer. • The thickness of the outer layer remains consistent across different morphologies on the bed particle surface (i.e., convexes and concaves), ensuring an almost uniform coverage across the entire bed particle. • Due to the uniform and nearly complete coverage of the bed particle surface, the outward migration of Fe is effectively hindered. ■ AUTHOR INFORMATION Corresponding Author Ali Valizadeh − Energy Engineering, Division of Energy Science, Luleå University of Technology, Luleå SE-971 87, Sweden; orcid.org/0000-0003-1203-0410; Email: ali.valizadeh@ ltu.se 25578 https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.5c01057 ACS Omega 2025, 10, 25569−25580

gasification technology represents a pivotal method for the clean and efficient utilization of coal, enabling the conversion of coal to high-value-added products such as syngas and fuel gas. This technology is extensively applied in critical areas, including power generation and chemical synthesis,1 providing essential support for the low-carbon utilization of coal resources. However, the process generates a significant amount of solid waste, specifically coal gasification coarse slag (CS), characterized by its complex composition.2 CS primarily consists of incompletely gasified residual carbon (a combustible phase) and aluminosilicate minerals (inorganic ash).3,4 The direct stockpiling or inefficient disposal practices of CS not only occupy valuable land resources but also pose risks of soil and water pollution from heavy metal leaching and the leaching of soluble salts. This issue has become a major bottleneck constraining the large-scale deployment of coal gasification technology.5 Consequently, enhancing the resource utilization of coal gasification coarse slag has emerged as a © 2026 The Authors. Unlike previous studies that mainly focused on elemental distribution or combustion characteristics, the present work systematically elucidates the occurrence morphology of carbon and ash and establishes the relationship between the occurrence modes and resource utilization potential. On the basis of this, this study focuses on coal gasification coarse slag from a Jinhua furnace, following 40 s of grinding. Different particle-size samples (CS60 to CS200) were obtained through sieving. Combined with multidimensional characterization methods, the influence patterns of particle size on the occurrence forms, composition, structure, and physicochemical properties of carbon and ash in coarse slag were systematically investigated, aiming to provide a theoretical basis for the graded and targeted utilization of coarse slag. Micromorphology. During coal gasification, inorganic minerals in coal typically aggregate into spherical or irregular blocky particles with smooth surfaces upon melting and cooling, driven by turbulence and surface tension, whereas incompletely gasified residual char predominantly exhibits a dispersed flocculent morphology.25 SEM images of parent CS and size-fractionated CS are presented in Figure 4. Three distinct characteristic particle morphologies are observed: dense/smooth irregular blocky/flaky particles (type A), porous irregular flocculent particles (type B), and dense/smooth spherical particles (type C). The surface micromorphologies of the size-fractionated CS samples varied markedly, generally exhibiting intermixed, adhered, or encapsulated states. The CS60 fraction (Figure 4b1−3) predominantly comprised largesized type A and C particles, indicating high inorganic ash content. Conclusions Three crude slags (CS-SH, CS-YK, CS-TY) exhibit diﬀerences in composition and structure characteristics, leading to distinct performance in thermal cracking, combustion, and adsorption. This study lls the existing research gap and veries that gasier type exerts systematic regulation on slag microscopic structure, further determining the optimal resource utilization pathway of each residue. CS-SH features higher xed carbon content (42.31%) and specic surface area (153.23 m2 g−1), exhibiting a “carboncoated ash” structure, presenting lower rst-order reaction activation energy (81.41 kJ mol−1) and higher comprehensive combustion index (1.6 × 10−7%2 min−2$°C−3), which makes it suitable for applications in gas adsorption, wastewater treatment and co-combustion fuel elds. CS-YK shows higher ash content of 98.47%, primarily composed of

reaction activation energy (81.41 kJ mol−1) and higher comprehensive combustion index (1.6 × 10−7%2 min−2$°C−3), which makes it suitable for applications in gas adsorption, wastewater treatment and co-combustion fuel elds. CS-YK shows higher ash content of 98.47%, primarily composed of inorganic minerals such as SiO2, Al2O3, and Fe2O3. Additionally, this residue demonstrates remarkable activation energies of 44.18 kJ mol−1 (n = 3) and 110.21 kJ mol−1 (n = 1) for thermal cracking and combustion, and lower comprehensive combustion index (2.33 × 10−10%2 min−2$°C−3), making it as a high-quality building material for cement admixtures or ceramic production. The ash content of CS-TY is as high as 93.26%, mainly composed of SiO2 and Al2O3. The carbon particles in this sample are wrapped by dense mineral layer, forming an “ashcoated carbon” structure, restricting adsorption and combustion performance. In addition, it can be used as raw material for heat-resistant building materials. Furthermore, CS-TY has a SiO2/Al2O3 ratio of 2.5, which makes it a candidate for preparing high-performance porous material such as molecular sieve. Regenerative thermal oxidizers (RTOs) have demonstrated VOC removal efficiencies of up to 99% and are widely used in industrial settings. RTOs can be classified into two structural types: cuboid and cylindrical. The cuboid RTO includes an equal number of intake and exhaust regenerative chambers, along with a purge chamber. The most common configuration is the 3-bed (regenerative chamber) RTO, although 5-bed RTOs are also in use.11,12 In particular, 3-bed RTOs have been studied extensively. Research has focused on the effects of switching time, regenerator height, velocity, temperature in the regenerative chamber, and VOC concentrations on the flow and heat transfer.13−15 By optimizing these parameters, the RTO can maintain self-combustion and achieve high thermal efficiency under low VOC concentrations.13 Each regenerative chamber alternates between intake, purge, and exhaust periods. Residual VOCs in the regenerative chamber during the intake period are flushed into the combustion chamber using an air purge, which prevents their release into the exhaust gas and improves the VOC removal efficiency. However, heat absorption by the purge air reduces the thermal efficiency of the RTO. These RTOs feature two regenerative chambers for the intake and exhaust, accounting for 4/5 of the total number of chambers, significantly more than in the 3-bed RTO (2/3 of the total chamber count). Although R-RTOs have been widely adopted in industrial applications, research on this configuration remains limited. Current simulation studies typically model only the regenerative and combustion chambers, without analyzing the complete R-RTO system or accounting for the effects of rotor rotation. Moreover, studies on plate-type regenerators are also scarce. Therefore, after validating the simulation model, this study investigates the flow and temperature distributions within the full R-RTO system and explores the heat transfer behavior within the plate-type regenerator. To address these gaps, the purpose of this study is to establish and validate a numerical model for the complete R-RTO, clarify the effects of rotary-valve switching on the internal flow field, temperature distribution, residence-time behavior, and VOC removal stability, and evaluate the heat-transfer performance of the plate-type regenerator under typical operating parameters. The results are expected to provide guidance for improving flow uniformity, reducing short-circuiting during valve rotation, and optimizing regenerator design for industrial R-RTO applications. CONCLUSION The R-RTO was developed based on the RTO used in a colorcoating line. Following verification with experimental results, the velocity and temperature distributions within the R-RTO were analyzed. The heat transfer behavior within the regenerator channels was also investigated. The following conclusions are drawn: The velocity distribution in the lower region of the RRTO�comprising the stator, rotary valve, and cone� was highly nonuniform. In contrast, both the velocity and temperature were uniform across the cross-section of the regenerative chamber. The velocity in the regenerative chamber increased from bottom to top owing to temperature-induced density variations. Within the combustion chamber, the velocity and temperature exhibited steep gradients as a result of flow redirection. The velocity and temperature fields in both the regenerative and combustion chambers varied periodically as the rotary valve switched positions. Although the average residence time in the combustion chamber was relatively long, 7.57% of the gas experienced residence times shorter than 1 s due to the influence of nonuniform velocity distribution. The rotary valve remained stationary for 17 s before rotating

the average residence time in the combustion chamber was relatively long, 7.57% of the gas experienced residence times shorter than 1 s due to the influence of nonuniform velocity distribution. The rotary valve remained stationary for 17 s before rotating for 2.5 s. During the stationary phase, the differences between inlet and outlet pressure, flow rate, and VOC removal efficiency varied minimally. However, during valve rotation, both the pressure difference and flow rate fluctuated significantly, and the VOC removal efficiency declined, negatively affecting the operational stability of the R-RTO. The temperature distribution within the plate-type regenerator remained uniform. For common R-RTO parameters-namely, regenerator height, switching time, and inlet velocity-values were selected within typical engineering ranges. The analysis indicated that these three parameters had limited impact on overall thermal efficiency, but their effects on heat transfer capacity were different. Among them, inlet velocity had the greatest influence on heat transfer and should be optimized together with pressure drop and fan power. Increasing regenerator height reduced the heat transfer coefficient and is therefore not recommended as the primary method for improving performance. Increasing regenerator height reduced the heat transfer coefficient and is therefore not recommended as the primary method for improving performance. Switching time had little influence on the heat transfer coefficient and heat transfer rate, although moderate extension can slightly improve thermal efficiency. For the present plate-type regenerator, a moderate height of about 1.2−1.5 m and an inlet velocity near 1.5 m/s are suggested as a practical compromise. The direct addition of dry clay to the metal ion solution and the use of ultrasonication to speed up the homogenization and intercalation steps were adopted from previous studies.34 The precursor salts, namely, aluminum sulfate hexadecahydrate (Al2(SO4)3·16H2O) and iron(II) sulfate heptahydrate (FeSO4· 7H2O), were used

clay to the metal ion solution and the use of ultrasonication to speed up the homogenization and intercalation steps were adopted from previous studies.34 The precursor salts, namely, aluminum sulfate hexadecahydrate (Al2(SO4)3·16H2O) and iron(II) sulfate heptahydrate (FeSO4· 7H2O), were used as sources of Al and Fe, respectively. The Al and Fe solutions were prepared by slowly adding 0.4 M NaOH solution to either 0.4 M Al or Fe solutions, using Al2(SO4)3· 16H2O and FeSO4·7H2O as sources, at a NaOH/Al or NaOH/Fe molar ratios of 2:1 (post reaction pH: Al = 3.32, Fe = 7.61). The solutions underwent continuous vigorous stirring at room temperature for 2 h, followed by ultrasonication for 30 min. CAA is a powerful tool which enables elucidation of current stability or kinetic reaction information. Thus, it reveals bubble effects on the stability of the current or its dynamics. For example, a reaction with a faster rate produces gas bubbles which have a negligible time of residence at the electrode surface, whereas a slow kinetic reaction rate tends to produce bubbles with significant residence time.
