The shift in basal spacing confirmed the success of the modification process. Enhancement in the BET surface area upon calcination, along with a decrease in pore size and an increase in pore volume, resulted in the more exposure of the Fe-BC active sites and the formation of loosely packed clay layers, thereby facilitating the mass transfer of reactants during hydrogen production. After lacing with Ag, the performance of the Fe-clay material improved significantly (about 21% increase in hydrogen production and 134% increase in TOF at −0.60 V applied potential vs RHE). By employing the frequency response technique, we have achieved the discrimination of multiple kinetic processes simultaneously occurring within the hierarchical pore networks of catalyst particles. This work conrmed that the diﬀusion processes within the macropores/mesopores of the matrix and the molecular exchange between the matrix and zeolite pores constitute the rate-controlling steps for mass transfer inside FCC catalyst particles.17 The above research results have preliminarily conrmed that a complex and interesting mass transfer behavior is observed in the FCC catalyst particles. According to previous studies,30 within an FCC catalyst microsphere, the molecular sieve, substrate, and other auxiliary components are primarily in a random distribution, resulting in a robust disordered pore structure. Notably, the molecular sieve serves as the primary active component of the FCC catalyst and is randomly distributed throughout the microspheres. Consequently, accessibility of the active components of the molecular sieve to heavy oil macromolecules has become a critical factor in determining the cracking activity of the catalyst. This accessibility heavily relies on the mass transfer performance of heavy oil macromolecules on the catalyst surface. The challenge of toxicity bioavailability of CNTs The high toxicity and low aqueous solubility of CNTs are their main limitations for biomedical applications. Due to their highly hydrophobic surface structures, CNTs exhibit very low solubility in most solvents, both organic and inorganic. Enhancing the solubility of CNTs in aqueous solutions is essential for their application in biological systems. There are two principal methods for functionalizing CNTs: covalent and non-covalent functionalization. Covalent functionalization involves chemically bonding functional groups to the CNT surface, which can signicantly alter their intrinsic properties. This method typically leads to improved solubility and reduced toxicity as it introduces hydrophilic groups that enhance dispersion in aqueous solutions.41 On the other hand, non-covalent functionalization relies on physical interactions, such as p–p stacking, van der Waals forces, and electrostatic interactions, to attach functional molecules to the CNTs without altering their core structure. This method preserves the inherent electrical and mechanical properties of CNTs while still enhancing their solubility and biocompatibility. Both functionalization techniques are crucial in tailoring the properties of CNTs to meet specic requirements in various biomedical and industrial applications.28,42 Although the mentioned factors have a similar nal inuence on living cells, their destructive function are not identical. This process helps to break up aggregates and ensure that the CNTs are evenly distributed. Surfactants or polymers are oen added during ultrasonication to stabilize the dispersed CNTs through non-covalent interactions. The energy from the ultrasonic waves facilitates the adsorption of these stabilizing agents onto the CNT surfaces, enhancing their solubility and preventing re-aggregation. In next stage, the mixture is subjected to centrifugation. This step separates the well-dispersed, functionalized CNTs from any remaining large aggregates or unfunctionalized CNTs. During centrifugation, the centrifugal force causes the denser, unmodied aggregates to settle at the bottom of the centrifuge tube, while the stabilized, functionalized CNTs remain in the supernatant. In this review, we examined the potential of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) in designing transmembrane channels to enhance the mass transfer through the cells' lipid bilayer membrane. Our analysis highlighted the signicance of the CNT length, noting that while shorter CNTs can serve as stable membrane channels, longer CNTs tend to become obstructed within the hydrophobic regions of the cell membrane. This insight underscored the importance of optimizing CNT length for eﬀective membrane integration. Furthermore, we explored the impact of surface functionalization on CNT permeability. The previous research results indicated that pure CNTs can readily penetrate plasma membranes without specic orientations, oen causing membrane disruption. In contrast, functionalized CNTs demonstrated a preference for vertical alignment, which minimized membrane damage and reduces energy barriers. The density and type of functional groups, such as carboxylic and amine groups, played a crucial role in maintaining this vertical

disruption. In contrast, functionalized CNTs demonstrated a preference for vertical alignment, which minimized membrane damage and reduces energy barriers. The density and type of functional groups, such as carboxylic and amine groups, played a crucial role in maintaining this vertical orientation and ensuring stable insertion into lipid membranes. The study concludes that functionalized CNTs, with their ability to maintain vertical congurations and reduce membrane perturbation, are proper candidates for acting as synthetic channels in the cell membrane. To overcome current barriers in the practical application of CNT-based membrane channels, future research should also prioritize the integration of CNTs with living systems by improving biocompatibility and minimizing cytotoxicity, which can be achieved through advanced surface functionalization and biomimetic coatings. Moreover, scalable and reproducible fabrication techniques need to be developed to enable large-scale production of uniform CNT channels with controlled length and functionalization patterns. Finally, exploring responsive gating mechanisms, such as stimuli-responsive functional groups or external control via electric or optical signals, could provide dynamic regulation of channel permeability, enhancing their utility in smart drug delivery and biosensing applications. Paper 2 Methods and materials 2.1. Synthesis of the PB from corn cob waste The biochar was synthesized at 600 °C, as described in our recent paper.20 2.2. Synthesis of the CD from corn cob waste The CD were synthesized by a hydrothermal method according to the procedure reported previously,29 with some modications described below. First, 50 mL of distilled water was added to 0.5 g of corn cob powder and stirred for 70 min. The homogeneous suspension was placed in an 80 mL Teon beaker of an autoclave, and hydrothermal treatment was carried out for 12 hours at a temperature of 180 °C. Then the content of the Teon beaker was cooled down to room temperature, transferred to centrifuge tubes, and centrifuged twice for 30 min at 5500 rpm. Aer decantation, the resulting solution was ltered through a paper lter. Subsequent centrifugation under the same conditions did not result in the formation of a precipitate. The solution of CD was brown-yellow in color and exhibited yellowgreen luminescence under UV light. 2.3. Overall, the comparative analysis demonstrated that carbonaceous nanoparticles/materials derived from corn cob waste exhibited markedly diﬀerent biocompatibility proles and opposite eﬀects on Cu2+-induced neurotoxicity. The divergent eﬀects observed between the PB and the other two materials underscore the importance of “safe-by-design” principles in the valorization of agricultural waste. While hydrothermal synthesis (CD) and open burning smoke collection (SP) are technically “green” or simple approaches, they may yield materials with inherent bioactivity that compromises their safety in biological environments. Transforming corn cob waste into the pyrolytic biochar (PB), however, shows a dual benet: it eﬀectively converts corn cob waste into functional carbon materials while mitigating environmental and health risks, providing a safe, neuroprotective material capable of mitigating Cu2+ toxicity. From an environmental perspective, the results underscore that not all carbonaceous materials derived from agricultural waste are equally safe for biological systems, even when produced using “green” methodologies. While the PB appears suitable for applications involving heavy metal sequestration with minimal neurobiological risks, CD and SP require careful toxicological evaluation before being considered for environmental or biomedical uses. However, due to the limitation of the in vitro synaptosomal model used in this study, further detailed in vivo exposure experiments using rodents are necessary to support biomedical translational claims. Although isolated synaptosomes provide a sensitive and mechanistically informative model of presynaptic function, extrapolation to in vivo systems should be made. Future studies should address long-term exposure, nanoparticle/material internalization pathways, and the role of protein corona formation in modulating nanoparticle–neuron interactions. Additionally, systematic characterization of the surface chemistry and metal-binding mechanisms of each nanoparticle and material will be essential to optimize the balance between the adsorption capacity and the neurobiological safety. Further studies are needed to clarify the relationship between the structural characteristics of biochars (surface functional groups, pore size distribution, and aromaticity) and their neuroprotective potential. The liquid product obtained from the pyrolysis process was analyzed using NMR spectroscopy and GC-MS, revealing that acidic groups, ketones, and aromatic compounds predominate in the bio-oil, while alcohols were present in smaller amounts. The effective diffusivity (Deff) of moisture during drying was low, suggesting that moisture moves slowly through the peel, which may contribute to the formation of distinct phases in the bio-oil. The obtained diffusivity and activation energy values indicate that moisture transport during drying was diffusion-controlled rather than reactioncontrolled. The bio-oil composition analysis showed that hightemperature drying conditions (C) maximized bio-oil yield. The findings suggest that controlled drying of yellow passion fruit peels around 423 K with 1 h of biomass drying optimizes bio-oil production,

This article is licensed under CC-BY 4.0 http://pubs.acs.org/journal/acsodf Article Analysis of Apparent and True Kinetics in Batch Circulation Reactor Systems Reinaldo Giudici* Cite This: ACS Omega 2026, 11, 55903−55909 ACCESS Read Online Metrics & More Article Recommendations ABSTRACT: Kinetic parameter determination in tubular reactors coupled with recirculation tanks is often complicated by kinetic disguises arising from simplified data treatment. When the reaction occurs solely in the tubular reactor but concentration measurements are taken in the stirred tank, treating the system as a batch reactor leads to falsified apparent kinetic parameters. Here we analyze this configuration using asymptotic methods for zeroth-, first-, second- and nth- order kinetics, deriving simple equations that relate apparent kinetic parameters to their true values. These relationships enable correction of falsified parameters under defined conditions, revealing that at low conversion per pass, reaction order remains accurate while rate constants are underestimated, whereas at high conversion per pass, the apparent kinetics shifts to first-order with rate constants governed by tank dynamics. This work provides practical tools for accurate kinetic analysis in batch recirculation reactors, improving reactor design and kinetic modeling. 1. INTRODUCTION Kinetic disguising can occur when the observed kinetics is treated using a simplified rate equation that do not account for the rigorous description of the key rate-determining steps, which may be of physical and/or chemical nature.1 The falsification (disguising) of kinetic parameters can occur in various situations, particularly when the analysis of experimental data relies on assumptions that are not strictly valid under the actual experimental conditions. The resulting model, being incomplete or oversimplified, transfers any errors from these invalid assumptions to the values of the effective (or apparent) kinetic parameters obtained. Consequently, the kinetic parameters thus determined�referred to as apparent or effective parameters�will be falsified. Understanding “disguised” kinetics is important for several reasons.1 Reliable rate equations and accurate kinetic parameters are essential for reactor design. Furthermore, developing robust kinetic models requires first demonstrating the ability to measure fundamental rate constants for both kinetic and transport steps.1 In many experimental studies of photocatalyzed reactions, concentration versus time data plotted on a semilog scale often appear linear, leading to the claim of apparent first-order kinetics. However, when the initial concentration of the reagent is varied, the apparent rate constant obtained from the slope of this plot often depends on the initial concentration,2 clearly indicating that the true kinetics are not first-order and that some form of falsification has occurred. Additionally, the occurrence of parallel reactions such as catalyst deactivation can cause kinetic disguise.8−11 In particular, the effects of falsification in the kinetics of heterogeneous catalytic reactions due to internal and external mass transfer are well known and discussed in classical Chemical Reaction Engineering textbooks.12−14 Experimental systems used to study the kinetics of homogeneous and heterogeneous photochemical reactions can have various designs. One of the most commonly used systems15−24 is a lighted tubular reactor in which the fluid recirculates to a coupled, dark stirred tank�a configuration also known as a batch reactor operating in circulation mode. The fluid is pumped from an agitated standby tank through the tubular reactor and then returns to the tank. This reactor system (a combination of a tubular reactor and a recirculation tank) is commonly used to study the degradation of contaminants by photochemical processes such as UV photolysis, UV/H2O2, and photoFenton.25−31 This experimental setup is also widely used in electrochemical reactors, sonochemical reactors, hydrodynamic cavitational reactors, fixed-bed catalytic reactors with recirculation, and solar reactors for microalgae cultivation. This configuration, with a tubular reactor coupled to a recirculation tank, is widely used because reagents can be fed and samples can be easily taken from the stirred tank, avoiding the more complicated process of sampling directly from the tubular reactor. Additionally, the tubular reactor can be constructed from glass or quartz with a small diameter, which, in the case of photochemical reactions, helps minimize or even neglect heterogeneity in the light field distribution across the tube’s cross section under appropriate conditions. The external recirculation also facilitates better temperature control when combined with an appropriate external heat exchanger, especially in cases involving intense radiation or significant heat dissipation phenomena such as ultrasound, electrochemical, or hydrodynamic cavitation in the tubular reactor. Besides photochemical reactors, this configuration is also commonly used in fixed-bed catalytic reactors with recirculation and sampling stirred tanks, as well as in other types of tubular reactors (sonochemical, cavitational, electrochemical, etc.) coupled to a recirculation tank. However, special care must be taken when analyzing data collected on the concentration of the reagent in the tank over time. If the data are analyzed by treating the entire system as a batch reactor (as sometimes occurs), while the reaction actually takes place only in the tubular reactor (and not in the recirculation tank), then this approach will introduce errors into the analysis, resulting in falsified values for the kinetic parameters. Previous works in the literature32−34 have discussed this problem of falsification of the kinetic parameters for small conversions per pass in the tubular reactor, and provided correction formulas for this regime, considering a Langmuir− Hinshelwood (LH) kinetics and their limiting cases of first- and zeroth-order reactions. DBD (dielectric discharge barrier), a type of non-thermal plasma, has been intensively investigated for plasma-catalytic DRM reactions.4–13 The integration of low-temperature plasma with heterogeneous catalysis is regarded as synergistically enhancing the CH4 and CO2 conversions, and improving product selectivity, stability and sintering tolerance. Ni-based catalysts are the most common ones employed in catalytic DRM reaction, due to their promising activity and selectivity, inexpensive price and widespread availability.2 Many researchers have been conducted to improve catalyst deactivation and increase catalytic performance on Ni-based catalysts3 and SiO2-supported Ni catalyst.14–18 SiO2 ber (SF) is an attractive support material due to its non-porous structure, contributing to easy accessibility and exposed active sites. Fiber-like structure supports e.g. SiO2 ber,18–21 CeO2 ber22 and ZSM-5 ber23 were studied in previous researches. Wen et al.18 reported the SiO2 nanobre conned Ni catalyst can improve Ni dispersion, leading to slightly higher initial activity and much better stability than Ni on commercial SiO2 powder support for CO2 reforming of methane process. Herminio et al.22 reported that Ni/ CeO2 brous catalyst for CO2 reforming of methane showed high resistance against carbon formation and enhanced catalyst stability aer 30 hours at 700 °C. The Fig. 1 Paper eﬀects of packing congurations of catalyst, amount of Ni loading on SiO2 support, catalyst support type, and applied voltage were evaluated. 2 Experimental 2.1 SiO2 ber (SF) preparation SiO2 ber was synthesized by sol–gel assisted electrospinning technique using tetraethyl orthosilicate (99.0% TEOS, Si(OC2H5)4) purchased from Sigma-Aldrich as a Si source. TEOS was dissolved in deionized water (DI water) with a 1 : 2 ratio followed by 37% HCl and 99.9% ethanol with a 0.01 : 2 ratio under stirring at room temperature. Aer that, the solution was continuously stirred and heated at 55 °C to form the gel. Paper 4 Conclusions The comprehensive study on the planar plate DBD plasmaassisted dry reforming of methane over Ni/SiO2 ber catalyst claried the factors aﬀecting overall system performance. Notably, catalysts supported on SiO2 ber exhibited superior catalytic performance compared to those on porous SiO2 pellets. Furthermore, the packing conguration within the plasma reactor was highly inuential, with a partial packing of the catalyst in the plasma zone demonstrating a signicant enhancement in system performance. This improvement is attributed to superior discharge distribution and stable plasma behavior. The applied electrical voltage strongly impacted both system eﬃciency and plasma discharge stability. Post-reaction characterization via TGA, Raman spectroscopy, XRD, and TEM-EDS conrmed the negligibly small level of coking on the catalyst surface and the structural integrity of the silica ber support under plasma discharge conditions. The optimum operational conditions for syngas production—achieving maximum CH4 and CO2 conversions, syngas yield, H2/CO molar ratio, and energy eﬃciency—were identied as 10% Ni/SF catalyst partially packed within the plasma reactor zone at an applied voltage of 15 kV. INTRODUCTION Mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana Linn) is a plant predominantly found in Southeast Asian countries, particularly Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia. Currently, it stands as one of Thailand’s most significant fruits, with a production of 251,635 tons in 2022.1 The pericarp of mangosteen is rich in several important bioactive compounds, including α-mangostin, β-mangostin, and γ-mangostin, all of which are xanthone derivatives. These compounds possess various pharmacological properties, such as antibacterial,2 antiviral,3,4 and antifungalactivities.5,6 Furthermore, mangosteen extracts exhibit anti-inflammatory effects. Chen et al. (2008) investigated the anti-inflammatory activity of mangosteen pericarp extracts, isolating α-mangostin and γ-mangostin. Additionally, α-mangostin demonstrated significant anti-inflammatory activity in carrageenan-induced paw edema in mice, substantially reducing swelling. These findings suggest that α-mangostin exhibits superior antiinflammatory efficacy compared to γ-mangostin.7 Given its potent anti−inflammatory properties, α-mangostin has garnered considerable interest for its potential in various cancer treatments. The detailed procedures are as follows: 3.1. Production of Xanthone Powder. The raw material for xanthone powder production is mangosteen peel powder, prepared through a series of processes including drying, size reduction, and sieving. Analysis of compounds in mangosteen peel extract revealed a mixture of both highly polar and less polar compounds as shown in the HPLC chromatogram (Figure 2). Specifically, highly polar compounds were observed on the left side of the chromatogram, while less polar compounds were on the right. The target compound, alphamangostin, was located in the middle, leaning toward the less polar group. Therefore, achieving high purity of alphamangostin necessitated the removal of as many other compounds as possible. CONCLUSIONS Mangosteen pericarp has been successfully utilized as a raw material for the production of high-purity alpha-mangostin. The initial extraction involved a percolation system using organic solvents, followed by reverse-phase column chromatography for preliminary separation. A key step in enhancing purity involved washing the extract with water and hexane to remove impurities before subsequent extraction with acetonitrile, also via percolation. This xanthone-rich extract was then fed into a Preparative Liquid Chromatography (C18 reverse-phase) system for further purification. This study investigates the optimization of boron extraction from the weakly alkaline brine of the Laguocuo Salt Lake (LGCSL) in Tibet, China, a representative of Tibetan weakly alkaline salt lakes. We evaluated the eﬃcacy of 2,2,4trimethyl-1,3-pentanediol (TMPD) as an extractant within a solvent mixture of 2-butyl-1-octanol (C12– OH) and sulfonated kerosene. The extraction performance was systematically assessed through singlestage and multi-stage counter-current extraction experiments, examining variables such as extractant type, concentration, pH, temperature, and the presence of co-existing ions. Our results demonstrate that optimal boron extraction is achieved under conditions of pH 8.0, an organic-to-aqueous phase ratio (O/ A) of 1 : 1.5, and lower temperatures. China's boron reserves rank fourth in the world.1 It has the characteristic of concentrated distribution of boron resources. 97% of the identied resource reserves are distributed in Tibet Autonomous Region (37%), Liaoning Province (34%), Qinghai Province and Hubei Province. Among them, sedimentary reworked boron resources account for 38% of the total, salt lake-type boron ore resource reserves account for 52% of the total, and other types account for 10%.2 The majority of liquid brine boron resources are located on the Qinghai and Tibet Plateau. Subsequently, the organic phase (marked as O2) in the second separatory funnel was precisely transferred to the third separatory funnel using a separatory funnel, and at the same time, the aqueous phase (marked as A2) was transferred to the rst separatory funnel. Striping extraction experiment 3.2.1. Selection of stripping agent. Stripping, also known as back-extraction, is the process where a stripping agent is used to move the extracted substance from the loaded organic phase back into the aqueous phase. This step is pivotal within the extraction process. It impacts not only the recovery rate of metal ions but also the overall eﬃciency and economic viability of the operation. The stage of extracting boric acid with 2,2,4trimethyl-1,3-pentanediol (TMPD) to generate borate is an esterication reaction process, while the stripping stage is the hydrolysis process of borate. From a molecular perspective, during the extraction process, TMPD forms a complex containing C–O–B ester bonds with boric acid, enabling boron to be extracted into the organic phase. Under alkaline conditions, the reaction of OH− with the boron–ester complex promotes

From a molecular perspective, during the extraction process, TMPD forms a complex containing C–O–B ester bonds with boric acid, enabling boron to be extracted into the organic phase. Under alkaline conditions, the reaction of OH− with the boron–ester complex promotes the cleavage of the ester bond, thus transferring boron back from the organic phase to the aqueous phase and achieving the separation of boron. Conclusion Taking the C12–OH solution of 2,2,4-trimethyl-1,3-pentanediol (TMPD) and sulfonated kerosene as extractants and taking the Laguocuo Salt Lake, a typical representative of weakly alkaline salt lakes in Tibet, as the research object, the process of extracting boron by TMPD was systematically studied. In the extraction process, one molecule of TMPD reacts with one boric acid molecule to form a complex containing two C–O–B ester bonds. In the case of high concentrations of CO32− and OH− ions in brine, it has a greater impact on the boron extraction rate. When the concentrations of carbonate and bicarbonate ions are high, boric acid mainly exists in the forms of [B4O5(OH)4]2− and [B(OH)4]−, and a small part is [B3O3(OH)4]−; these forms of borate ions are diﬃcult to combine with TMPD, so the extraction rate is low. The above was characterized by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy and Raman spectroscopy, providing the mechanism of this reaction. In the extraction process research, through single-stage and multi-stage countercurrent extraction experiments, the eﬀects of diﬀerent extractants, extractant concentration, pH value, temperature, and coexisting ions on the extraction eﬃciency were investigated, and the appropriate extraction conditions were determined. The results show that under

process research, through single-stage and multi-stage countercurrent extraction experiments, the eﬀects of diﬀerent extractants, extractant concentration, pH value, temperature, and coexisting ions on the extraction eﬃciency were investigated, and the appropriate extraction conditions were determined. The results show that under the conditions of pH = 8.0, O/A = 1/1.5, and lower temperature, the boron recovery rate is relatively ideal. The single-stage boron extraction rate is >83%, and the three-stage boron extraction rate is 98.61%. At the same time, the stripping experiment results show that NaOH is a suitable stripping agent. When the NaOH concentration is 0.3 mol L−1 and the phase ratio is 2 : 1, the stripping eﬀect is good at room temperature, and the boron concentration is also enriched. The research results provide a theoretical and experimental basis for recovering boron from weakly alkaline salt lake brine and verify the feasibility of this method. Pyrolysis is the most interesting of these conversion routes because it may turn waste biomass into high-value energy products including bio-oil, pyrogas, and solid biochar. Biochar has been used for more than only improving soil in the last several years.20 Recent studies have shown the adaptability of biomass derived biochar in sophisticated environmental and applications such as wastewater treatment,21,22phytoremediation23 and catalysis.24,25 To engineer biochar with the specic physicochemical properties required for these advanced applications and to maximize energy yields precise control over the thermal degradation process is non-negotiable. This necessitates a profound understanding of thermal degradation kinetics. Kinetic parameters (activation energy, preexponential factors) serve as the mathematical backbone for predicting biomass behavior under thermal stress. A signicant body of literature has examined the pyrolytic behavior of various feedstocks to derive these parameters.26–28 They examined the pyrolytic behavior of biomass and derived kinetic parameters based on which the thermodynamic parameters were established. The kinetic analysis revealed that SGSW decomposition is governed by a multi-stage mechanism with average activation energy. 50–70 kJ mol−1 across diﬀerent models indicate favorable energy requirements for thermal conversion compared to several other biomass feedstocks. In conclusion, the integration of the circular economy into bioenergy is essential for achieving sustainable resource utilization. Gasification, anaerobic digestion, and chemical looping processes provide a viable pathway for converting biomass and industrial waste into valuable energy products. The policy framework should be strengthened to promote the valorization of agricultural residues and industrial byproducts, thereby encouraging the rural economy to adopt the waste-to-wealth concept and accelerating the shift from fossil to renewable biobased alternatives. Integration of biowaste to the gasification process aligns with the carbon-neutral approach and toward the sustainable developmental goals.108,109 The gasification process integrated with biological pretreatment offers a holistic route to utilize various biological substances in the form of both feedstock and microbial sources. Wastewater treatment techniques Conventional water treatment technologies such as coagulation, ltration, occulation, sedimentation, and others have been reported to be ineﬀective in remediating water containing sulfonamides.23 Also, the possibility of utilising physical methods such as adsorption has been investigated.40–42 However, adsorption cannot break down sulfonamides in water but only transfers it from one medium to another leading to secondary pollution. Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) such as the electrochemical oxidation process,43 Fenton/photo-Fenton,44 photocatalytic process,45 cavitation-based AOPs,46 and radiation-enhanced catalytic reaction47 have proven to be eﬀective treatment techniques with the ability to breakdown sulfonamides in water, but they suﬀer some setbacks. For example, electrochemical oxidation methods rely on the use of electrical energy to produce radicals that can degrade pollutants, but this technique is impeded by factors such as electrode lifetime, increased current density, the electrical conductivity of the electrode, as well as the possibility of the electrode undergoing fouling because of the presence of organic deposits on the electrode surface. In addition, it oﬀers high degradation eﬃciency, low temperature, less energy demand, solar utilization, mild reaction conditions, zero sludge formation, and easy catalyst recovery.50 3.1 Photoelectrocatalytic oxidation: overview In addition to other details not specically mentioned earlier on various AOPs, the PEC process has been identied as an eﬃcient technology in the treatment of water polluted with antibiotics.52 This is because of the synergistic eﬀects of both the electrochemical oxidation and photocatalytic degradation processes.53 The PEC process is based on the application of bias potential to facilitate the migration of the photogenerated electrons from the conduction band of the photoanodes towards the cathode, thereby giving the photogenerated holes the ease to react directly with the pollutant and degrade them. Also, the photogenerated holes can react directly with water molecules to produce hydroxyl radicals which also complements the degradation process. In addition, the rate of recombination is suppressed due to the application of bias potential, the powdered photocatalyst is easy to recover since they have been immobilised on a substrate, and the recycling eﬃciency of the photocatalyst is enhanced.54 Overall, the PEC process presents itself as a promising and highly eﬃcient technology. PEC has been applied towards the abatement of diﬀerent emerging pharmaceutical pollutants such as ciprooxacin, tetracycline, paracetamol/acetaminophen, and diclofenac, among others. Light plays a signicant role in the PEC process as it promotes the excitation of the photogenerated electrons from the valence band to the conduction band of the semiconductor materials. Therefore, the choice of semiconductor materials is based partly on their light-harvesting properties. Some materials absorb more in the UV region of the electromagnetic spectrum, examples include TiO2,14 ZnO,55 BiPO4,56 etc., while some materials absorb more in the visible spectrum. The conventional light sources for the PEC oxidation of sulfamethoxazole (and other pharmaceuticals) include UV-A lamps,50,61 mercury lamps,7 and xenon light.2 Recently, researchers have used green light emitting diode (LED) as their light source for the PEC degradation of sulfamethoxazole.19,54,59,62 LED possesses some merits over other light sources because it is cheaper, less toxic, less energy consuming, low production of heat, small in size, and possesses a longer lifetime. These merits place LED-based systems at an advantage for future application in the PEC technology for the removal of sulfamethoxazole and other pollutants in general. 3.1.3 Nature of the substrate or the electrode. Practical challenges and stability considerations Practical durability and environmental relevance are still understudied in many studies, despite the large body of research on performance improvements attained by the integration of green additives. Oxidative attack, hydrolysis, and mechanical fatigue from fouling and cleaning cycles are known to age and degrade polymer membranes during operation; these processes can change their pore structure, hydrophilicity, and mechanical integrity over time, ultimately aﬀecting ux and selectivity during long-term service. Furthermore, under continuous ltration conditions, additives incorporated in the polymer matrix, particularly inorganic nanoparticles, may leach out; reported instances of nanoparticle loss may have an impact on the eﬄuent quality and membrane performance.104 Lastly, most published studies use synthetic dye solutions or model solutes, which do not accurately reect the complexity of actual wastewater matrices with mixed organic matter, ions, and biological constituents; membranes frequently perform diﬀerently when tested under actual eﬄuent conditions, indicating a disconnect between laboratory evaluations and real-world applications.105 To increase the translational impact of green additive techniques, it is necessary to perform long-term stability testing, leaching assessments, and validation in actual wastewater systems. Smart and responsive green additives The next development in sustainable membrane engineering is represented by smart and responsive green additives, which combine the usefulness of stimulus-responsive systems with the environmental advantages of bio-derived materials. Smart green additives can actively react to changes in the pH, temperature, light, or ionic strength, in contrast to conventional plant-based or natural additives, which passively improve hydrophilicity or antifouling qualities. Membranes may adjust in real time to changing feedwater conditions thanks to this dynamic behavior, which improves selectivity, lowers fouling, and increases long-term operating stability. When functionalized or coupled with bio-inspired motifs, biopolymers, including chitosan, alginate, tannic acid, and cellulose derivatives, provide reversible swelling, charge-switching, or conformation modications that control water transport and pollutant interactions. Incorporating these clever green materials into polymeric membranes oﬀers a new route towards high-performance, energy-eﬃcient, and self-regulating separation technologies, in addition to being consistent with circular and ecofriendly design concepts. As research progresses, smart green additives are anticipated to be a key component in the creation of next-generation membranes that are suited to intricate and changing water treatment problems.117 RSC Adv., 2026, 16, 22166–22185 | 22177

Mechanism Through processes that activate in response to certain environmental stimuli, smart and responsive green additives improve membrane performance and allow membranes to dynamically adapt during ltration. The chemical functionality of bio-based compounds, including polysaccharides, polyphenols, and bio-inspired moieties, as well as their capacity to experience reversible structural or charge changes, gives rise to these mechanisms. The following are the important mechanisms:118–120 10.1. Functional group ionization that responds to the pH Functional groups (–COOH, –OH, –NH2, and phenolic groups) found in many green additives undergo protonation or deprotonation based on pH. These groups become protonated at low pH, which lessens the negative charge and electrostatic repulsion between foulants and the membrane surface. Deprotonation enhances hydrophilicity and repels charged impurities by increasing the surface charge density at high pH. The membrane can transition between compact and swollen states thanks to this reversible ionization, which enhances pollutant rejection and permits natural self-cleaning. 10.2. Changes in the temperature-responsive conformation Certain bio-based additives show thermo-responsive behavior, in which temperature changes cause polymer chains to expand or contract. Hydrophilic groups dominate below a certain temperature, improving permeability and water uptake. Hydrophobic interactions intensify above this temperature, tightening the pore architecture and decreasing

bio-based additives show thermo-responsive behavior, in which temperature changes cause polymer chains to expand or contract. Hydrophilic groups dominate below a certain temperature, improving permeability and water uptake. Hydrophobic interactions intensify above this temperature, tightening the pore architecture and decreasing fouling. Membranes can control the ux based on the temperature thanks to this process. 10.3. Structural rearrangement that responds to redox Green additives that are rich in phenolic compounds, such as catechols and tannic acid, can undergo reversible oxidation and reduction, allowing surface charge, crosslinking, or switchable adhesion. Quinone formation via oxidation encourages surface stiﬀness and crosslinking. Reduction increases hydrophilicity and protein-repelling behavior by restoring catechol groups. 10.4. Reversible switching between hydrophilicity and hydrophobicity In reaction to environmental stimuli, certain smart additives change the surface energy of the membrane. Increased hydrophilicity during ltration (better ow) and increased hydrophobicity aer ltration (better fouling release) are the two possible outcomes. 11. Thermo-responsive behavior in green membranes Synthetic polymers with a sharp, lower or upper critical solution temperature (LCST/UCST), like poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) 22178 | RSC Adv., 2026, 16, 22166–22185 Review (PNIPAM), are traditionally linked to thermo-responsive behavior in membrane systems, where reversible hydration– dehydration transitions result in noticeable changes in wettability and permeability. Conversely,

or upper critical solution temperature (LCST/UCST), like poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) 22178 | RSC Adv., 2026, 16, 22166–22185 Review (PNIPAM), are traditionally linked to thermo-responsive behavior in membrane systems, where reversible hydration– dehydration transitions result in noticeable changes in wettability and permeability. Conversely, the majority of native biopolymers (e.g., cellulose, chitosan, alginate, starch, and proteins) lack sharp and reversible LCST/UCST transitions in water due to their rigid hydrogen-bonded structures, wide molecular weight variability, and strong intermolecular forces.121,122 Therefore, thermo-responsiveness in so-called green or bio-based membranes usually results from biosynthetic hybrid systems, in which thermo-responsive synthetic segments (most oen PNIPAM or PNIPAM-like moieties) are chemically graed, blended, or copolymerized with biopolymers acting as sustainable backbones or supports. The temperature-triggered switching capability of these systems is provided by the graed synthetic component, while the biopolymer provides mechanical stability, hydrophilicity, and environmental compatibility. Therefore, reported thermoresponsive eﬀects in green membranes are engineered properties rather than inherent characteristics of unmodied biopolymers, and their practical applicability depends on the graing density, cycling stability, transition sharpness, and long-term resistance to oxidative and thermal degradation.123,124 12. Functional group chemistry and its role in membrane performance The functional group chemistry introduced in the membrane matrix can be used to explain the observed antifouling and separation performance. The observed antifouling behavior and separation eﬃciency can be fundamentally attributed to the tailored functional group chemistry incorporated within the membrane matrix. Strong hydrogen bonds with water molecules are encouraged by hydrophilic moieties like hydroxyl and carboxyl groups, which result in the creation of a stable hydration layer at the membrane surface. This hydration layer improves antifouling behavior by acting as an energy barrier against microbial adhesion and the adsorption of organic foulants. Molecular level interactions orchestrate the balance between permeability and selectivity by modulating surface charge via ionizable functional groups, which repel similarly charged foulants, minimize pore blockage, and enhance contaminant rejection. Concurrently, intrinsic antibacterial and radical-scavenging properties suppress oxidative degradation and biolm formation, preserving pore integrity and sustaining long-term membrane performance.125,126 13. It is particularly challenging to quantitatively validate sustainability claims regarding energy usage, emissions, toxicity, and end-oflife impacts because there are currently few comparative life cycle assessment (LCA) studies on green membranes than on conventional membranes. Furthermore, there are still obvious trade-oﬀs between performance and sustainability because improvements in hydrophilicity and antifouling behavior may jeopardize chemical stability, mechanical strength, or longterm durability under practical operating conditions. The majority of antifouling chemicals used today are synthetic and perhaps dangerous, which raises issues for wastewater contamination, occupational exposure, and the release of nanoparticles during production, use, and disposal. On the other hand, natural or green additives like plant extracts, biopolymers, and materials produced from waste oﬀer lowtoxicity, renewable substitutes that frequently have several uses, such as metal-binding ability, hydrophilicity, antibacterial activity, and antioxidant behavior. Nevertheless, insuﬃcient mechanistic knowledge of long-term fouling resistance, membrane aging, biodegradation, and additive leaching prevents their practical implementation. Membrane integrity can be compromised, permeability reduced, and performance unpredictable due to nonuniform dispersion within polymer matrices, heat and solvent instability during phase inversion, and agglomeration at high loading levels. membranes in water treatment, reviewing the various methods used to modify them to improve permeability and reduce surface fouling. These methods include traditional approaches such as blending, surface coating, and graing, which have contributed to improving the operational properties of membranes. However, due to the drawbacks of traditional methods, researchers are focusing on biological systems and preferring green synthesis. Recent studies have focused on the use of environmentally friendly materials as additives in membrane development due to their biodegradability, low toxicity, and natural availability. CBM has been exploited commercially in the USA, Canada, and Australia, optimizing the fossil energy consumption structures.5−7 CBM resources in China are abundant, but affected by multiple tectonic movements and high stresses, the in situ coal permeability is mostly low, restricting gas migration, resulting in low CBM production in many areas.8−10 Therefore, enhancing the in situ permeability of coal is critical for efficient CBM exploitation. Compared with the method primarily utilized in CBM exploitation (hydraulic fracturing), chemical treatment (acidization and oxidation) can enhance the permeability of coal on a large scale. Coal is mainly composed of organic matter and minerals, and minerals (especially carbonate and silicate minerals) dissolved by acid to form new pores and fractures can enhance the permeability. In the last decade, NPs of precious metals such as gold (Au), silver (Ag), and platinum (Pt) have been extensively explored due to their potential application in catalysis.11–14 Many studies have indicated that the performance of NPs strongly depends on their size and shape.15,16 Smaller particles have a larger specic surface area and more active sites on the surface, and hence exhibit superior activity.17 Unfortunately, small-sized nanocatalysts easily agglomerate owing to the high surface free energy, which greatly reduces their catalytic performance.18,19 In order to prevent the agglomeration of nanocatalysts, supports with a certain stability, larger specic surface area, and good adsorption capacity, including mesoporous silica (mSiO2),20 magnesium oxide (MgO),21 titanium dioxide (TiO2)22 and graphene oxide (GO), have been introduced to achieve good dispersion of metal NPs.23 Supports like m-SiO2 and MgO are able to increase the specic surface area and provide additional RSC Adv., 2026, 16, 63091–63102 | 63091

Paper RSC Advances Fig. 11 Schematic diagram of the catalytic reduction mechanism. 4 Conclusion In summary, a facile co-reduction process for the synthesis of Ni–Ag/rGO nanocomposites was proposed using rGO as a support for the Ni/Ag bimetal. Catalysts with diﬀerent weight fractions of GO were synthesized, and the eﬀect of the amount of rGO on the catalytic performance was studied. Ni–Ag/rGO nanocomposites with a moderate amount of rGO support prevented the agglomeration of the NPs and signicantly improved the catalytic activity of the catalyst. Owing to the SMSI eﬀect and uniform dispersion induced by rGO, the Ni–Ag/rGO catalyst with 0.5 wt% GO showed the highest rate constant towards the reduction of 4-NP, which was 3.4 times that without GO. The enhanced catalytic activity of the Ni–Ag/rGO catalyst with 0.5 wt% GO could be attributed to the improved dispersion of the Ni–Ag bimetallic NPs and acceleration of electron transfer between the catalyst and rGO. The Ni–Ag/rGO catalyst also exhibits good magnetic recyclability and stability, with only 8% loss aer 10 cycles, providing a potential solution for treating 4NP in practical applications. INTRODUCTION Carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) are vital strategies for mitigating carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions and combating climate change. Gas hydrate-based carbon capture is a promising approach within the CCUS framework, offering a potentially efficient and long-term storage solution for captured CO2. In the context of CCUS, gas hydrate-based carbon capture involves the formation of CO2 hydrates, where CO2 molecules are trapped within a lattice of water molecules under high pressure and low temperatures.1−4 One of the key advantages of gas hydrate-based carbon capture within the CCUS framework is its potential for long-term storage. Once the CO2 is captured and converted into hydrates, it can remain stable for extended periods, reducing the risk of leakage of the CO2 into the atmosphere. PROCESS OF HYDRATE-BASED CARBON CAPTURE Gas hydrate nucleation is a sophisticated microscopic process that begins with the initial aggregation of hydrate nuclei and continues with their expansion to a critical size that supports sustained growth. This complex sequence is influenced by various thermodynamic and kinetic factors and is characterized by stochastic and time-dependent properties. A critical metric in assessing hydrate nucleation is the induction time, which measures the period from the onset of gas−water cluster formation to the point where these clusters stabilize into a critical size. Induction time is a vital indicator of the occurrence of nucleation and is subject to influence by several variables, including chemical composition, system configuration, and mixing conditions.13−16 The shorter induction time suggests more favorable thermodynamic and kinetic conditions for rapid hydrate formation. The stochastic nature of hydrate formation is attributed to the system’s metastability, defined as the ability of a nonequilibrium state to persist in a seemingly stable condition over prolonged durations. In the nucleation phase, water molecules assemble around guest atoms or molecules to form either incomplete or complete crystalline embryos. There are two types of additives, generally termed as promoters, which include kinetic and thermodynamic promoters. Thermodynamic promoters are utilized in hydrate formation as they shift the equilibrium, which means they reduce the high pressure to lower required for hydrate formation. In contrast, kinetic promoters (commonly “surfactants” or “amino acids”) alter the interfacial properties during gas/liquid contact, due to which increased hydrate formation rates are achieved. These kinetic promoters have no effect on the phase equilibrium curve.63 The thermodynamic and kinetic promoters can be used together, which is termed the synergistic effect of promoters on hydrate formation. Thermodynamic promoters shift equilibrium conditions to milder temperature−pressure regimes, while kinetic promoters accelerate hydrate formation rates by improving interfacial characteristics and reducing induction times. This results in significant enhancement of hydrate formation kinetics, lowering the required pressure, improving hydrate selectivity, and reducing overall energy costs. Following the completion of hydrate nucleation, hydrate growth takes place. This growth process depicts the growth of stable hydrate nuclei into solid hydrates. The growth of hydrate depends upon temperature, pressure, agitation, interfacial area, and degree of subcooling. When there is a sudden sharp drop in the pressure caused by the consumption of gas molecules, it shows hydrate formation and growth, and the constant pressure in the system depicts the completion of the hydrate formation process. In addition to this, a sudden rise in temperature of the system represents hydrate formation as it is an exothermic process, while a constant temperature marks the completion of the hydrate formation process.47 There are key kinetic parameters that are studied for hydrate growth, which include 1. The third common type of gas hydrate reactor is the spray tower. By scattering water into a continuous gas phase region, the gas/water interfacial area can readily be increased. Likewise, as the tiny water drops have a large speed in the gas phase of the reactor, the necessity of a mechanical stir system is ruled out for this type of reactor. MACHINE LEARNING AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR CO2-BASED GAS HYDRATE FORMATION Carbon dioxide (CO2) hydrate formation simulation is a critical area in the advancement of carbon capture and storage (CCS) technologies. Gas hydrates, which are crystalline waterbased solids physically resembling ice, form when gas molecules, such as CO2, are trapped within cages of hydrogen-bonded water molecules. CO2 hydrates have gained considerable attention for their application in carbon sequestration due to their capacity to stably store CO2 under high-pressure and low-temperature conditions. CONCLUSIONS By effectively capturing and storing carbon dioxide (CO2) over an extended period of time, gas hydrate-based carbon capture and storage (CCUS) technologies represent a promising solution to the urgent problem of climate change. Recent developments in CO2 hydrate formation research, the technoeconomic aspects of CCUS plant operations, and the incorporation of hydrate-based capture into more comprehensive decarbonization plans have all been methodically reviewed in this review. Notably, the study also examined the new models and simulations of CO2 hydrate formation processes using machine learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques, highlighting their potential to speed up design optimization and lower experimental costs. Although hydrate-based CCUS has clear benefits, such as high selectivity and the potential for energy-efficient operations, a number of technical, financial, and computational issues must be resolved before its full potential can be realized. INTRODUCTION The terahertz (THz) frequency range (0.1−10 THz) has become a focus of research because of its broad potential in areas such as noninvasive imaging, spectroscopy, and emerging wireless communication. One of the major challenges in advancing THz technology is the lack of materials and device platforms that can dynamically control electromagnetic waves in this spectral window.1,2 Phase-change materials (PCMs) have emerged as a strong candidate, as their reversible transition between amorphous and crystalline phases leads to pronounced changes in both optical and electrical properties.3−5 Among materials investigated for THz tunability, vanadium dioxide (VO2) has been frequently employed as a representative PCM due to its sharp and reversible metal−insulator transition near 68 °C, producing strong modulation of electrical and optical properties. ACS Omega http://pubs.acs.org/journal/acsodf Article Sn incorporation alters the crystallization behavior of GST, modifying its transformation pathway rather than directly improving crystallinity. Diffraction analysis reveals the coexistence of several crystalline phases, mainly SnTe and SnSb, together with residual GST reflections, indicating that Sn atoms tend to bond preferentially with Te and Sb during thermal processing. Such mixed-phase formation suggests that Sn changes the atomic rearrangement dynamics and promotes heterogeneous nucleation within the film. The relatively low bond dissociation energy of the Sn−Te bond (359.8 kJ mol−1) compared with the Ge−Te bond (456 kJ mol−1) further facilitates bond rupture and atomic diffusion during annealing. Consequently, crystallization begins at a lower temperature, governed by the emergence of Sn-rich phases with weaker bonding strength. CONCLUSIONS This work examined GST and Sn-incorporated GST thin films deposited on alumina substrate to understand the influence of Sn on structure and THz performance for tunable THz sensing. FE-SEM revealed rough surface roughness, while EDS confirmed that Sn content increased with sputtering power. The GIXRD result showed that Sn modifies the crystalline route of GST, forming mixed SnTe and SnSb phases together with residual GST, indicating preferential bonding between Sn, Te, and Sb that enables phase formation at lower temperatures through weak Sn−Te bonds. XPS spectra further supported this trend, showing a downward

of GST, forming mixed SnTe and SnSb phases together with residual GST, indicating preferential bonding between Sn, Te, and Sb that enables phase formation at lower temperatures through weak Sn−Te bonds. XPS spectra further supported this trend, showing a downward shift in the Te 3d peaks, suggesting an evolution toward increased metallic character and modified local bonding environments involving Sn−Te interactions. It should be noted that XPS primarily probes surface chemical states, while GIXRD reflects bulk structural phases; thus, the combined results provide complementary insight into Sn-induced phase evolution and bonding behavior. THz-TDS analysis demonstrated strong dielectric contrast between amorphous and crystalline states, with Sn incorporation amplifying the tunability. Simulations of SRR metasurfaces using measured dielectric data showed a resonance shift of about 0.16 THz from phase transition GST thin films. Additionally, Sn-incorporated GST could improve modulation efficiency with reduced thermal input. Overall, Sn incorporation provides a practical route to control phase evolution and resonance behavior in GST-based materials, contributing to advancing tunable THz photonics devices. representative waste generated during urban wastewater treatment. It is characterized by high moisture content, high ash content, and complex composition. Sewage sludge contains recoverable organic matter, nitrogen, and phosphorus, while also concentrating potentially hazardous heavy metals such as Zn, Cu, Pb, Cr, Ni, Cd, and As. Improper disposal can therefore cause resource loss, heavy metal release, and secondary pollution risks.1,2 Compared with landfilling, composting, and direct incineration, gasification converts the organic fraction of sludge into combustible gases such as H2, CO, and CH4 under oxygen-deficient or oxygenlimited conditions, while most inorganic constituents are retained in solid residues. Gasification is therefore considered an important thermochemical route for sludge volume reduction, energy recovery, and inorganic resource recovery.2−4 However, sludge gasification should be evaluated not only in terms of syngas quality and energy conversion efficiency but also in terms of heavy metal stability and leaching risk in the gasification residues. waste coutilization. Carbide slag is a large-volume alkaline industrial solid waste produced during acetylene or poly(vinyl chloride) production using the calcium carbide route. Carbide slag typically contains Ca(OH)2, CaCO3, CaO, and other calcium-based constituents and is characterized by high calcium content, high alkalinity, and low cost. As a waste-derived calcium source, carbide slag has the potential to replace part of commercial CaO in sorption-enhanced gasification. Han et al.14 used bauxitemodified carbide slag for calcium-looping gasification of sewage sludge and found that it increased H2 yield and gasification efficiency, mainly through in situ CO2 capture by calcium-based components and gasification enhancement. In coal and biomass systems, carbide slag has also been shown to promote steam gasification, enhance hydrogen-rich gas generation, and exhibit potential for CO2 capture and multicycle gasification.15−17 These studies indicate that carbide slag has a sound basis for process intensification in steam gasification systems. However, sewage sludge differs from coal and common biomass because of its high ash, high phosphorus, and heavy metal contents. The role of carbide slag should therefore not be interpreted only from the perspective of gas-phase product regulation. The environmental behavior of heavy metals is an important consideration during the thermochemical conversion of sewage sludge. During gasification, some semivolatile elements may migrate to fly ash, condensates, or the gas phase as temperature increases, whereas others remain in bottom residues. Their environmental risk depends on chemical speciation and leaching behavior. Ewald et al.18 investigated entrained-flow gasification of sewage sludge and found that Hg, Tl, Cd, Pb, As, Zn, Cu, and Ni volatilized to different extents, while inorganic constituents such as P and K were mainly enriched in gasification ash. Further research has shown that temperature, reaction atmosphere, and additives affect heavy metal evaporation and retention during sludge gasification.19 Other studies have emphasized that the environmental risk of heavy metals in sludge pyrolysis or gasification residues should not be assessed only by total concentrations but should be evaluated using chemical speciation, leaching concentrations, and risk indices.20 Minerals and Ca-containing additives, including CaO, montmorillonite, calcium aluminosilicates, and calcium phosphates, have been shown

sludge pyrolysis or gasification residues should not be assessed only by total concentrations but should be evaluated using chemical speciation, leaching concentrations, and risk indices.20 Minerals and Ca-containing additives, including CaO, montmorillonite, calcium aluminosilicates, and calcium phosphates, have been shown to affect heavy metal volatilization, speciation transformation, and leaching risk during sludge thermal treatment.21−24 BCR sequential extraction, TCLP leaching tests, and RAC risk assessment are commonly used to evaluate the potential mobility and environmental safety of heavy metals in sludge thermaltreatment residues.25 It is therefore necessary to clarify whether carbide slag can simultaneously enhance hydrogen-rich gas generation and decrease the active fractions and leaching risks of heavy metals in gasification residues. Current studies on carbide slag-enhanced sludge gasification mainly focus on H2 generation and CO2 capture, whereas a systematic understanding of the apparent retention, speciation transformation, and leaching risks of heavy metals in gasification residues remains limited. In particular, direct experimental evidence is still lacking on whether hydrogenrich gas production and heavy metal stabilization can be synchronously regulated under different carbide slag dosages and gasification temperatures. The aim of this study was to elucidate the mechanistic divergence and ozone mass-transfer behavior in photocatalytic ozonation systems employing bimetallic Pd/Cu-modified TiO2 and C3N4. Specifically, the study sought to i) compare the pathways of ozone activation and pollutant transformation; ii) assess the role of reactive oxygen species versus non-ROS mechanisms in the degradation of antibiotics and ARGs; iii) evaluate the relationship between catalyst loading, degradation kinetics, and post-treatment biological inactivation; and iv) critically examine the influence of scavenger compounds and dissolved organic matter on ozone consumption and mechanistic interpretation under environmentally relevant conditions. Photocatalytic ozonation, an innovative AOP process that merges photocatalysis and ozonation, has garnered significant attention as a potent technique for degrading organic contaminants in water. The prominent aspect of this technique is its high efficiency in pollutant degradation with a limited amount of byproducts compared to traditional water treatment methods. In the typical photocatalytic ozonation process, a photon is absorbed by the photocatalyst, which leads to electron−hole separation. Then, ozone absorbs these newly created electrons/holes, and, after a series of reactions, produces various ROS.7−9 The key parameters influencing this process are an appropriate band gap, a low recombination rate, and ozone and pollutant adsorption capabilities.7,9 Therefore, among the plethora of available photocatalytic materials, titanium dioxide (TiO2) and graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4 or simply C3N4) have emerged as frontrunners due to their exceptional photocatalytic properties. Both materials exhibit different decontamination behavior while used in the photocatalytic ozonation process. The photocatalytic activity of TiO2 primarily involves the generation of electron−hole pairs upon light absorption with simultaneous adsorption of ozone molecules, followed by redox reactions that lead to the formation of surface-bound ozone species, which are later transformed into ROS. TiO2 primarily involves the generation of electron−hole pairs upon light absorption with simultaneous adsorption of ozone molecules, followed by redox reactions that lead to the formation of surface-bound ozone species, which are later transformed into ROS. These interactions result in large amounts of ROS in the form of hydroxyl radicals, bound hydroxyl radicals, and/or positive holes. The ozone species and newly created ROS can react with organic pollutants or participate in redox reactions, contributing to the degradation process.6,10 The degradation activity depends on the crystal structure of TiO2, and it is believed that although rutile generates more hydroxyl radical species, they are strongly bound to the catalyst, leading to overall poorer performance.6 On the other hand, C3N4, due to the higher-lying conduction band (−1.3 V in comparison to −0.1 V vs NHE for C3N4 and TiO2, respectively), exhibits a different reaction pathway in photocatalytic ozonation. When exposed to ozone molecules, first O2●− species are formed, which consequently react with O3 causing formation of O3●− which further are transformed into hydroxyl radicals; in addition, during photocatalytic oxidation, ●OH are formed from O2●− and H2O2.11,12 All of these ROS play a crucial role in oxidizing organic pollutants, facilitating their degradation into harmless

causing formation of O3●− which further are transformed into hydroxyl radicals; in addition, during photocatalytic oxidation, ●OH are formed from O2●− and H2O2.11,12 All of these ROS play a crucial role in oxidizing organic pollutants, facilitating their degradation into harmless byproducts. Despite their differences in ROS production, both catalysts share some similarities. TiO2 and C3N4 are known for their reasonable cost, abundance, chemical photostability, semiconductive character, and the possibility to tailor their properties according to needs.13−15 Unfortunately, both materials are also characterized by high recombination rates of electrons/holes. In addition, in the case of TiO2, the band gap is ∼3.2 eV,8 which limits the utilization of sunlight to ∼5% (the percentage of UV in the sunlight spectrum reaching Earth’s surface16). On the other hand, C3N4 possesses a highlaying valence band which hinders its catalytic activity.17 Therefore, strategies like doping with foreign metals have been adopted to enhance the both of these materials’ photocatalytic activity. Technology, Karlsruhe 76131, Germany; DVGW German Technical and Scientific Association for Gas and Water Research Laboratories, Water Chemistry and Water Technology, Karlsruhe 76131, Germany CONCLUSIONS This study successfully elucidated the distinct mechanisms and efficiencies of bimetallic Pd/Cu-modified TiO2 and C3N4 catalysts in the photocatalytic ozonation of sulfamethoxazole (SMX) and antibiotic-resistant genes (ARGs). Both bimetallic catalysts significantly enhanced degradation rates compared to those of ozonation alone, with (Pd/Cu)C3N4 generally exhibiting higher pseudo-first-order rate constants than (Pd/ Cu)TiO2. The investigation of reaction mechanisms using radical scavengers revealed fundamental differences between the two materials. For C3N4-based photocatalytic ozonation specifically, superoxide radicals, singlet oxygen, and ozone play a dominant role in pollutant elimination. Conversely, TiO2based processes exhibited a different behavior, where ROS appeared less critical for the deactivation of specific targets like intl1, suggesting the involvement of alternative pathways such as direct hole or electron interactions. Furthermore, the study highlighted a trade-off between the removal efficiency and regrowth inhibition. While lower metal loadings (0.1 and 0.5 wt %) demonstrated the highest performance for the initial removal of ARGs, the 1 wt % Pd/ Cu loading was necessary to effectively prevent bacterial regrowth after treatment. Additionally, the efficiency of both systems was influenced by the water matrix; the presence of EfDOM in secondary effluents increased the required ozone dose by competing for oxidants and affecting the ozone decomposition profiles. Ultimately, (Pd/Cu)0.5%C3N4 demonstrated the best overall performance in enhancing ozone mass transfer and removing ARGs driven by its capacity to accelerate ozone consumption through a variety of ROS. These findings underscore that while both catalysts are effective, their optimal application depends on the specific target pollutants and the necessity of controlling bacterial regrowth with C3N4 showing particular promise for ROS-driven remediation strategies. ■ Complete contact information is available at: https://pubs.acs.org/10.1021/acsomega.6c09130 ASSOCIATED CONTENT Author Contributions sı Supporting Information * M.G. conceived and designed the project, conducted photocatalytic ozonation experiments, environmental sampling and analysis tests, and contributed to refining the final version of the manuscript. Pure corn straw fuel (SF) served as the control. The pyrolysis characteristics of both pellet fuels up to 1000 °C were systematically investigated via thermogravimetric (TG) analysis at heating rates of 10, 20, and 30 °C/min. The pyrolysis characteristics were analyzed via characteristic parameters, Gaussian fitting assignments, and the Flynn−Wall−Ozawa (FWO) and Kissinger− Akahira−Sunose (KAS) model-free kinetic methods. Within the tested temperature range (50−1000 °C), CF exhibited higher characteristic parameters than SF, suggesting facile initiation under the conditions tested. A positive deviation between the experimental and calculated TG curves preliminarily indicated a synergistic effect during the core copyrolysis stage (170−650 °C). the experimental and calculated TG curves preliminarily indicated a synergistic effect during the core copyrolysis stage (170−650 °C). Gaussian fitting was tentatively assigned to four bond cleavage stages for both fuels, with the cleavage of Cal−heteroatom bonds as the dominant reaction (proportion >50%). The addition of oil sludge introduced more alkyl-substituted aromatic compounds into CF, increasing the proportion of Car−Cal and Car−heteroatom bond cleavage from 6.8% (SF) to 15.8% (CF). The average apparent activation energy of CF was higher than that of SF. Notably, CF exhibited a kinetic characteristic of low initial activation energy and high overall activation energy, which favored facile pyrolysis initiation and inhibition of side reactions. 1. INTRODUCTION The intensifying global energy crisis has spurred significant research interest in recovering energy from solid wastes. Agricultural biomass, due to its abundance and carbon neutrality, has garnered widespread attention.1 While biopressed fuel is a common treatment, its low calorific value limits its high-value applications.2 Concurrently, oil sludge, a viscous, hazardous waste generated during petroleum production, storage, and transportation, contains substantial organic matter (e.g., hydrocarbons). Incineration and solvent extraction are conventional treatments, but high costs and environmental risks constrain their efficiency and sustainability.3 Pyrolysis is a thermochemical process that decomposes

Incineration and solvent extraction are conventional treatments, but high costs and environmental risks constrain their efficiency and sustainability.3 Pyrolysis is a thermochemical process that decomposes organic substances into valuable products under high-temperature and oxygen-free conditions.4,5 It has emerged as a promising and feasible technology for the efficient treatment of agricultural biomass and oil sludge.6−10 Copyrolysis, a process involving two or more feedstocks, can induce synergistic effects among the components.11,12 Copyrolysis of agricultural biomass and oil sludge can complement each other: biomass provides abundant volatiles, while oil sludge contributes a high calorific value and a stable carbon structure, potentially improving pyrolysis characteristics and product quality.13 Previous studies have explored various aspects of copyrolysis. Our previous work28 focused on the pelletization method and clarified an optimal preparation method for a composite pellet fuel (CF) derived from corn straw and oil sludge. Its thermochemical reactivity, component interaction mechanism, and intrinsic kinetic features remain unclear, which hinders the further engineering application of this waste-derived pellet fuel. This work emphasizes how oil sludge incorporation alters the pyrolysis behavior of the pellet fuels. The pyrolysis characteristics of the composite pellet fuel (CF) derived from corn straw and oil sludge are investigated and compared to those of conventional corn straw pellet fuel (SF). CONCLUSIONS In this study, the pyrolysis characteristics of SF and CF (corn straw/oil sludge = 60/40, w/w) were systematically investigated via TG experiments, combined with weight loss behaviors, their Gaussian-fitting results, and FWO/KAS kinetic analysis. Their pyrolysis characteristics were compared, with the main conclusions as follows: (1) SF and CF displayed outstanding weight loss behaviors in the range of 170−650 °C, and their weight loss obtained at different heating rates was all above 85%. Compared with SF, the overall reaction processes of CF shifted backward. Oil sludge improved the thermal stability and overall pyrolysis performance of corn straw fuel. The incorporation of oil sludge elevated the pyrolysis characteristic parameters of SF. (2) Synergistic effects (Δw > 0) existed between oil sludge and corn straw with the proceeding copyrolysis process (170−650 °C), with the experimental TG curve of CF higher than the calculated one. The Δw (Δw = +3.35%) exhibited a distinct maximum at approximately 460 °C, corresponding to the peak decomposition of heavy organics in oil sludge. (3) The bond cleavage reactions of SF and CF involved the release of free volatiles and cleavage of carboxyl, Cal− heteroatom, S−S, Cal−Cal, Car−Cal, and Car−heteroatom bonds, respectively.

Introduction Ammonia (NH3) is a cornerstone of modern society, serving as an indispensable precursor for nitrogen fertilizers and emerging as a highly promising zero-carbon fuel for energy storage. However, synthesizing NH3 by breaking the highly inert N^N triple bond remains one of the most energy-intensive challenges in chemical manufacturing. For over a century, global production has been dominated by the Haber–Bosch process, which catalytically combines N2 and H2 under extreme temperatures (400–650 °C) and pressures (200–400 atm).1 Consequently, this energy-intensive process accounts for approximately 2% of global energy consumption and 1.8% of global CO2 emissions, primarily due to the steam-reforming of methane for H2 production.2 Despite its high energy eﬃciency at large-scale production, the process still relies on centralized, continuous operations, presenting a signicant barrier to integrating intermittent renewable energy sources. Beyond optimizing the static properties of the electrolyte, dynamic regulation of the hydrodynamic boundary layer—through forced convection and viscosity tuning—represents a critical but underexplored aspect in Li-NRR. While proton and nitrogen supply are optimized in Li-NRR systems,18,25 the diﬀusion of nitrogen and protons to the Li-deposited cathodic surface can become rate-limiting steps in Li-NRR. This point is particularly relevant for phosphoniumbased shuttles, where high viscosity and molecular size introduce a mass-transport limitation that cannot be inferred from interfacial chemistry alone. Despite their stability advantages, the high viscosity associated with the [P6,6,6,14][NTf2] salt raised the question of how LiNRR performance changes when the phosphonium cation structure is varied. Current challenges of Li-NRR Despite the signicant progress made in optimizing electrolyte composition and SEI engineering, the Li-NRR process faces both fundamental and technological challenges that must be addressed for industrial-scale viability. 4.1. Energy eﬃciency limitation The most pressing concern is the inherently low energy eﬃciency (EE) of Li-NRR systems (Table 1).13,63,64 Currently reported EE ranges from 1–17% under realistic operating conditions, with a theoretical thermodynamic maximum ceiling of only 27.8%—a fundamental limitation set by the electrochemistry of lithium electrodeposition.13 This poor energy eﬃciency can be attributed to three factors: (1) the extreme negative potentials required for lithium electrodeposition (typically −3.2 to −4.6 V vs. SHE), leading to enormous overpotentials; (2) energy losses across the dynamic SEI; and (3) additional potential drop required to drive Li0/+ electroreduction via SEI. In comparison, the Haber–Bosch process achieves high energy eﬃciency of ca. 60% under optimized conditions. To make Li-NRR economically competitive for distributed ammonia electrosynthesis, the EE must be improved to above 40%, which requires new approaches beyond electrolyte optimization. Electrolytejsolvent decomposition Understanding solvent and electrolyte degradation in Li-NRR requires distinguishing between cathodic and anodic processes, as each proceeds through diﬀerent chemistry and inuences the system stability under diﬀerent conditions. At the cathode, the highly negative potentials required for Li deposition drive partial reductive decomposition of the lithium salt anion and, to a lesser extent, THF. However, owing to its RSC Adv., 2026, 16, 31426–31441 | 31437

Rather than being purely detrimental, this controlled partial decomposition of the salt anion and solvent at the onset of operation is mechanistically benecial via the SEI layer (see Section 2). At the anode, in contrast, degradation is far more severe and represents a stability issue in Li-NRR systems. Specically, THF—the standard solvent due to its high N2 solubility—undergoes oxidative polymerisation at high positive anodic potentials (>3 V vs. Li0/+).43,49 This anodic polymerisation generates byproducts that increase electrolyte viscosity, reduce ionic conductivity, and hinder ion transport.49 The cumulative result is system degradation and performance loss aer prolonged operation, which is commonly experienced in high-pressure batch cells.27,34 Recent advances using diglyme continuous-ow cells have achieved longer operation (300 h).13 The ether backbone of diglyme lacks the strained ring structure of THF and thus exhibits markedly superior resistance to anodic ring-opening polymerisation, though it presents challenges including higher viscosity and cost relative to THF.13 Despite its status as a “redox mediator,” lithium is not completely recovered aer

Multiple degradation pathways of lithium ions could occur simultaneously: (1) side reactions between electrodeposited Li0 and the organic electrolyte/solvent,31 forming stable lithium compounds (LiH, Li2O, Li2CO3, etc.) that are not electrochemically regenerated; (2) precipitation and encapsulation of lithium within thick, poorly conducting organic-rich SEI layers;31 and (3) mechanical loss through electrode fracturing and particle detachment during cell cycling.69 Over extended operation, these cumulative losses necessitate periodic electrolyte replacement, complicating system design. 4.3.
